paragraphs.text: After that he offered the burnt offering and sprinkled its blood round about on the bronze altar, while the flesh of the sacrifice he cut into pieces and washed and burned all of it on the altar.

entries.section: (1) Sacrifices for the priests and the people

paragraphs.text: After the priests offered sacrifices for themselves, they offered for the people a sin offering, which was the kid, and they burned all of it outside the camp and did not eat of it this time, because of the death of the two sons of Aaron for their sin (ch. 10:1, 2, 16-20), since they sinned during the seven days of their ordination and died.

entries.section: (1) Sacrifices for the priests and the people

paragraphs.text: Then he offered the burnt offering for the people and likewise the grain offering, for he took his handful of it and offered it on the altar, all these sacrifices in addition to the morning burnt offering that was offered before all the sacrifices offered for the priests or for the people.

entries.section: (1) Sacrifices for the priests and the people

paragraphs.text: Then he offered the peace offerings for the people, which were the bullock and the ram, and after slaughtering them he offered their fat on the altar, while their breasts were eaten by the priests and the rest of the flesh was probably eaten by the elders of the people on its behalf.

Offer repentance for your sins before you require it of those around you; it is good to teach those around you, but be an example to them in examining yourself and offering prayers and worship, and you will save your own soul and those for whom you are responsible.

entries.section: (2) The blessing and the holy fire

paragraphs.text: Came down: because the altar of burnt offering was three cubits high, about a meter and a half, and they would go up on it by a sloping surface, because the Law forbade the use of a ladder (Ex 20:26). The lifting of the hand to pronounce the ritual blessing (Num 6:22-26) represents the authority of the priesthood, and this blessing is completed after the offering of the sacrifice, because the blood of Christ is the foundation of every blessing. The Church has taken this, since at the end of every church service the priest raises his hand with the cross, giving the blessing of Christ to all the people before their departure.

entries.section: (2) The blessing and the holy fire

paragraphs.text: The entering of Moses, the chief of the prophets, with Aaron, the high priest, into the tabernacle means the importance of the word of God on the tongue of the apostles and prophets in the Holy Bible, and the importance of the work of the priesthood and the ritual of the Church for our salvation.

Thus the second blessing was completed, and their entering together was for Moses to hand over the rituals of the service to Aaron. The appearing of the glory of the Lord was perhaps in the form of a cloud or fire or incense or other spiritual phenomena, and this signifies the presence of Christ in the Church.
It is noted that the steps that took place before the appearing of the glory of God and what follows it are:
1- The offering of the sacrifices for the priests and the people.
2- Aaron's blessing of the people (v. 22).
3- Aaron's coming down from the bronze altar (v. 22).
4- The entering of Moses and Aaron into the sanctuary, perhaps so that Moses might explain and confirm to Aaron how to serve in the sanctuary (v. 23).
5- Their coming out from the sanctuary and their blessing of the people a second time (v. 23).
6- The appearing of the glory of the Lord, and this was the second time after its appearing at the completion of the setting up of the tabernacle (v. 23).
7- The coming out of fire from before God and its burning of the sacrifices (v. 24).
8- The people's bowing down and shouting (v. 24).

entries.section: (2) The blessing and the holy fire

paragraphs.text: Fire came out from before the Lord and extended to the altar and burned the sacrifices, for the Holy Spirit by His fire burns our sins and cleanses us. The shouting of the people is a proof of their joy in the Lord, while their bowing down is reverence and worship of Him. The appearing of the fire and its burning of the sacrifices means:
1- The greatness of God and His glory.
2- God's satisfaction with His people and His acceptance of their sacrifices.
3- God's confirmation of His covenant with His people by means of the sacrifices, which are a symbol of the sacrifice of Christ.
4- His acceptance of the service of the priests.

Hold fast to your spiritual worship and trust that God wants to appear in your life in different forms to reassure you and gladden your heart, so that you advance in your spiritual life and hold fast to Him more and more.

The death of the two sons of Aaron. This chapter shows us the attributes required of the priests of the Old Testament, which signify the attributes of the priests and servants of the New Testament. These attributes are:
1- Obedience 2- Rising above natural feelings
3- Not being occupied with anything other than the service 4- Not drinking intoxicants, and discernment and discrimination

entries.section: (1) The death of Nadab and Abihu

paragraphs.text: Censer: a metal vessel in which burning coal is placed with grains of incense (a thurible) on top. The two sons of Aaron the priest, "Nadab and Abihu," were so bold as to break God's law by offering strange fire inside the sanctuary, and they did not take from the divine fire that had come out from the tabernacle of the congregation to the bronze altar (ch. 9:24). This strange fire signifies the fire of the passions or the teachings foreign to the Church, with which we cannot enter before God.

In addition, offering incense in the censer was the work of the high priest, while the priests offered incense and fire in other holy vessels (Ex 30). The elders of the Jews think that they were in a state of drunkenness, because this chapter stipulates that the priest is not to be drunk (vv. 8, 9). It is very regrettable that two of the great ones of the people, who were priests, should fall into a clear violation of God's commands a very short time after their ordination.

Be careful about what you teach others, which is the teachings of the Church that you received from her, and if you do not know something, do not presume to give rulings or advice whose correctness you do not know, but ask those who are more experienced than you, and that not only in spiritual and church matters but in any subject of life, so that you are wise and people respect your opinion and you cause no one to stumble.

entries.section: (1) The death of Nadab and Abihu

paragraphs.text: We see here that the blessed fire of the Lord that accepted the sacrifices turns into a deadly fire to discipline the sinner, and this is a proof of God's justice and holiness and His anger at the errors of His servants. Aaron's shock was great, but he submitted in silence. And God declared through Moses that He requires holiness and precision in obeying His commandments from all people, especially those near to Him such as the priests, and if they break His commandments they are punished more severely because they know God more than others.

entries.section: (1) The death of Nadab and Abihu

paragraphs.text: Because it is not permitted for Aaron and his two remaining sons to take part in the procedures of mourning or burial, as they are occupied with their service, others of their relatives carried out the task, for the law of God requires that the priest not leave his service in the sanctuary for any reason however important, to show the greatness of God and His service. The two who buried Nadab and Abihu were their cousins, so Moses said to them "carry your brethren," since a cousin is called a brother, as it was said of the cousins of Christ that they were His brethren, and as is said now in the land of Egypt.

Nadab and Abihu were carried in their priestly garments, which were probably not burned by the fire, as a showing by God of the dignity of the priesthood, although this is contrary to the nature of fire, which burns everything before it.

entries.section: (1) The death of Nadab and Abihu

paragraphs.text: Moses commanded them to raise their feelings above the human level, as the Lord commanded Ezekiel the prophet at the death of his wife (Ezek 24:15-18), and not to practice the pagan customs in mourning for relatives, for the feelings of the priest belong first to God, and then to all people and are not limited to his relatives. The going out of the priests to bury Nadab and Abihu would prevent them from practicing their priestly service, since they would be made unclean by touching the dead as the Law prescribes, and there were no other priests. God also wished to show the heinousness of the sin of Nadab and Abihu in breaking God's law, so the people nearest to them, their father and their brothers, did not take part in burying them, but He allowed the whole people at the same time to take care of burying them and to weep for them in honor of their priesthood.
Despite the small number of consecrated priests, two of them died, for God is exacting in choosing His servants however great the need of the service.
Wine: grape juice that has fermented naturally.
Strong drink: grape juice fermented so strongly that it makes the one who drinks it drunk, and it was perhaps made by distilling wine.

God forbids His priests to drink wine of all kinds before they enter the service of the tabernacle of the congregation, as abstinence from material things and so that they may be fully alert, in sanctification and reverence of the house of God.
From here we conclude that what drove the two sons of Aaron to error was perhaps their drinking wine to the point of drunkenness.

The meaning of this is that, although the priests may drink a little wine, that is, naturally fermented grape juice, with a very small percentage of alcohol, in their ordinary life, this is not permitted before they enter the service, while intoxicating wine, that is, strongly fermented, is not permitted in any case.

By not drinking wine the priests keep their balance so that they can practice the function of discernment and teaching, so that they distinguish between the unclean and the clean and complete their service with concentration, and are also able to guide the people and teach them God's commandments and laws. Drunkenness signifies immersion in the things and pleasures of the world to the point of losing balance and spiritual discernment.

Use the material things of the world, for they are God's gift to you, but do not immerse yourself in them lest they distract you from God and all your thinking becomes about them and your view of everything becomes material, so that you no longer long for spiritual things, but your conduct changes and becomes carnal, far from God.

entries.section: (3) The priests' eating of their portion

paragraphs.text: Moses began to encourage Aaron and his sons to eat their portion of the offerings made by fire of the Lord (as explained before in ch. 8), because it seems that the grief in their hearts was intense over what had happened, and likewise their fear of God, and he confirmed the law, which is the eating of the unleavened bread in the house of the Lord (a holy place), and it is eaten by the priests only (ch. 6:14-18), while the priests' portion of the peace offerings, which is the right shoulder and the breast, they eat with their wives and sons and daughters in a clean place outside the tabernacle of the congregation.
Sin brings grief, but I must not stop at it; rather I wipe it away with repentance and regain my joy in the Lord.

entries.section: (4) The burning of the goat of the sin offering

paragraphs.text: The two remaining sons of Aaron erred in the ritual of the sin offering, for they did not eat their portion of it but burned it, so Moses was angry with them and rebuked them so that they would not neglect carrying out God's commands. This error is lighter than the error of their two brothers (v. 1), because the first was deliberate while this one was from forgetfulness. The priest's eating of the sin offering of the people was a proof of his sharing with his people in bearing their sin, and also that God had accepted the sacrifice and forgiven the sin (ch. 4:22, 27). And Moses reminded them that, as long as the blood of the goat of the sin offering was not brought into the sanctuary and the altar of incense anointed with it, the priest must eat his portion of it, from which it is understood that the priest's portion of the sin offering is not only permitted him to eat, but it is necessary that he eat it.

entries.section: (4) The burning of the goat of the sin offering

paragraphs.text: Such things have befallen me: the death of my two sons Nadab and Abihu.

Should it have been accepted in the sight of the Lord: Aaron asked whether God accepts that we eat of the sin offering while we are in grief over the death of Nadab and Abihu, or whether it would be considered an error, because we ought to eat of God's sacrifices with contentment and thanksgiving and joy, that is, he excuses himself for not eating of the goat lest he eat it in sorrow and sin against God. Aaron excused himself to Moses by saying that his two sons Eleazar and Ithamar had offered to the Lord the sacrifices that were required of them, but their state of mind, his and his sons', after what had befallen them of discipline from God by the death of their two brothers, did not allow them to share in eating of the sacrifice, because they felt they were bearing the sins of their two brothers who had died, so how could they bear with them the sins of the people and eat of the flesh of the goat? Therefore they left it to burn entirely on the bronze altar, and Moses accepted their excuse, because God bears the weakness of Eleazar and Ithamar but does not bear the pride of Nadab and Abihu.

Repentance washes away the sins of your shortcomings and neglect, so hasten to it that you may obtain forgiveness in the Sacrament of Confession and be strengthened to begin anew with care and vigor to make up for what you have missed, so that you grow in your love for God. Clean and unclean animals
Cheweth the cud: chews its food again after swallowing it to complete its digestion.

Hoof: the front of the animal's foot, which is either a single piece or cloven into two parts. The Book of Leviticus. God defined for Moses what is unclean and what is clean, as a Father concerned with every detail of our daily life. The definition included two conditions together, which are:
1- Chewing the cud, and this points to careful meditation on the meanings of the word of God.

2- The cloven hoof: which gives the animal the ability to walk for a longer time, so it signifies striving and perseverance in it. There is another opinion that the cloven hoof signifies discernment. The Book of Deuteronomy defined these clean animals (Deut 14).
I wish you would read the Holy Bible every day with care and understand its words and meditate on them to apply them in your life, and even repeat one verse throughout the day to live in it.
The coney: a small animal like the rabbit that lives in Palestine and dwells among the rocks, with sharp claws, and it signifies fierceness.

If the animal does not have the two preceding conditions, that is, if one of them is lacking, it is considered unclean. The camel and the coney and the hare do not have a cloven hoof, so they are not eaten, and the swine does not chew the cud, so it is considered unclean.

The hare and the coney are considered among the animals that chew the cud, since they move their jaws continually as though they were chewing the cud but without actual rumination, and this is because the commandment was given according to the way of life of the ordinary person and not according to specialized scientific study. The swine signifies uncleanness because of its wallowing in the mire and its eating of dirty foods.

The Law confirms not eating of the unclean animals even if one of the conditions is present in them, which is chewing the cud or the cloven hoof. And it forbids touching their carcasses after their death for two reasons:
1- The connection of death with sin, since it is a result of it when God declared that in Paradise, so touching the dead makes unclean.
2- A health benefit, because the carcass of an animal brings germs harmful to man.
Scales: the scales of fish.
It defines two conditions together for aquatic creatures:
1- The presence of fins, as a reference to strength in movement and the ability to swim against the current. These are traits of the spiritual man.

2- The presence of scales and shells that protect the body from the pressure of the water and the shocks of the rocks, as a reference to a person's resisting evil and fortifying himself with the various means of grace.

Those in which these two traits are present may be eaten, for they are clean, whereas those in which one of the two traits or both are lacking are considered unclean, so they are not eaten and touching their carcasses is not permitted.

Resist sin and keep away from its sources, and if you fall into it, rise quickly and do not despair, for your God loves you, and resistance is accomplished by prayer and reading and lowering yourself in humility before God with persistence until He rescues you from it, relying on the power of His Body and Blood.
The eagle: a large wild bird that snatches its prey, and it signifies theft.

The ossifrage: called the bearded vulture, it resembles the eagle, and it throws its victim from a height to shatter it, and it signifies cruelty. The osprey: a coastal bird that eats fish, and it signifies snatching.

The kite: a wild bird that lives by snatching and eating stinking carcasses, and it feeds on filth. The hawk: a wild bird of prey like the kite, with sharp sight. It signifies the use of gifts for evil. The raven: a wild bird that snatches prey and loves stinking carcasses, and it signifies theft and greed. The ostrich: a huge wild bird that does not sit on its eggs in the nest, and it signifies recklessness and not bearing responsibility.

The male ostrich: the male of the ostriches, which is more beautiful than the female. It signifies vain outward beauty. The gull: the seagull, a sea bird that snatches, which signifies theft and greed.
The falcon: like the hawk and used in hunting, and it signifies injustice.
The owl: a wild night bird, and it signifies ruin because of its living in ruins.
The cormorant: a coastal bird that dives to snatch fish, and it signifies theft.
The crane: a large long-legged bird that cries out much, and it signifies noise and restlessness. The pelican: a strong bird of prey that loves swimming, and it signifies fierceness.
Al-Qawq: a water bird like the swan, and it signifies ruin.
The vulture: a bird of prey like the eagle, and it signifies evil.
The stork: a bird that eats frogs and insects, long-beaked and long-legged. It signifies uncleanness and lack of care.
The parrot: a predatory bird that imitates speech, and it signifies lightness of mind.

The hoopoe: a skillful wild bird that eats worms and insects, and it signifies hypocrisy and outward beauty. The bat: one of the flying mammals, and it is a bird of prey, and among its kinds are blood-sucking ones, and it signifies parasitism.

It defines the traits of the unclean birds as being predatory, fierce in nature, and eating carrion, that is, stinking carcasses and filth, despite the beauty of their outward appearance. They point to the traits of the wicked and their hypocrisy as mentioned in the preceding description of the birds, and they show the necessity of the purity of the source of our teaching and our spiritual food, and the necessity of gentleness and of not harming others.
Leap: jump.
Creeping thing of the fowl: birds that walk on the ground with their feet.
Legs: the leg above the foot.
The locust, the bald locust, the beetle, the grasshopper: stages of the locust.

It adds a new attribute to the forbidden birds, which is the inability to fly and being content to walk on the ground, "creeping," as a reference to the lack of spiritual elevation and attachment to earthly things. As for insects, the flying are clean and the creeping unclean, for the same reason, which is that it signifies the lack of spiritual elevation.

The inspired text forbids eating the animals that do not have a cloven hoof or do not chew the cud, because they are unclean, and it also forbids touching their carcasses after their death lest a person become unclean.

It adds to the unclean animals those of the four-footed that go upon their paws, such as the dog and the cat and the mouse and the monkey, as a reference to the uncleanness of a person's being bound wholly to earthly things and attached to them. The Book of Leviticus. And whoever touches or carries the carcass of an unclean bird or animal becomes unclean until the evening, so that he feels the wrong of sin and keeps away from the evil traits of the forbidden animals, and then he washes himself and his clothes with water as a symbol of the water of Baptism and the Sacrament of Repentance and Confession.
As much as you think of heaven and care for prayer, you are able to give up your material attachments and evil desires, so that you gradually rise and advance with steady steps toward eternity.
The weasel: an animal like a large mouse that lives by snatching, and it signifies theft. The mouse: it signifies destruction.
The spiny-tailed lizard: a green desert animal with a strong tail like the crocodile, and it signifies violence.
The gecko-like lizard: like the gecko, and it signifies uncleanness and lack of care.
The monitor lizard: a crawling animal with a long snout and a long tail that eats eggs, and it is like the chameleon, and very hostile to snakes. It signifies theft.
The lizard: a kind of reptile like the chameleon or the crocodile, and it signifies preying.
The small lizard: a kind of reptile like the chameleon, and it signifies clinging to the earth.
The chameleon: a kind of reptile that changes color to the color of its surroundings, and it signifies hypocrisy.

God gives a statement of the small animals that walk on four feet and the unclean reptiles. We notice what they signify of the traits of the wicked as explained before, and their sharing the trait of clinging to earthly things, so whoever touches their carcasses becomes unclean until the evening.
Sack: haircloth (a garment) of camel's hair or goat's hair.

It confirms here that any articles used in the house, if the carcass of a creeping thing falls on them, become unclean, so they should be put into water until the evening to be cleansed, and so God commands keeping away from the carcasses of the unclean animals because they signify sin, since death entered the world through sin, and they also carry diseases or infection that call for cleaning and cleansing what their carcasses fall upon. And the power of water to cleanse is a symbol of the power of Baptism in the forgiveness of sins.

If the carcass of a creeping thing falls on an earthen vessel with any liquids in it, it becomes unclean, and since earthenware absorbs the liquids that became unclean, it must be got rid of by breaking it, and likewise whatever it contained, because it became unclean. Likewise the carcass of a creeping thing makes unclean any liquid or food it touches.
The Book of Leviticus
Oven: a furnace.
Range for pots: the stove that was used anciently for cooking and heating, which is a barrier of brick inside which fire is kindled, and on top of it the vessel to be heated is held.
Likewise the oven or the range on which it falls is broken down, because it has become unclean.

As for wells and springs, their water is renewed from the groundwater, so they become clean, because the water that became unclean is thrown on the ground and new water from the groundwater takes its place. And the part of the water that became unclean and fell on the ground is drained away with the earth it fell on and thrown far away because it has become unclean. Here the Law confirms the heinousness of sin and its uncleanness.

The water becomes unclean by the carcass of the animal, and then the seeds absorb this water and become unclean and must be got rid of, whereas dry ones, when the carcass of an animal touches them, remain clean, because the carcass touches their outer husk and they are considered clean, since the seed changes when it is planted and becomes a plant through food and water and sun.
Carcasses are unclean even if they are of clean animals, for they are a symbol of bearing sin.

We also see the action of water in cleansing as before, so whoever touches them or eats of them unwittingly, not knowing that it was dead, or carries its carcass, becomes unclean until the evening and must wash with water.

The uncleanness of the reptiles that cling to the earth in their going, like snakes, points to attachment to earthly things, and likewise everything that goes on four feet or more; all these animals are unclean and are not eaten, with the exception of the clean animals that go on four feet and were mentioned before, such as cattle and goats and sheep.

The purity of the children of God is required as a condition of their sonship to the holy God, who brought them out of the places of uncleanness and out of Egypt, the land of idols, to make them saints, so that they keep away from touching the carcasses of creeping things or anything unclean.

Thus this chapter distinguished between everything that is clean and what is unclean, and between everything that is eaten and what is not permitted to be eaten. As for the law of the New Testament, it considered all of God's creation clean according to the vision of the Apostle Peter (Acts 10:11-13), since our Baptism has cleansed us and raised us up with a new holy nature.

Let us examine ourselves daily and search our souls lest some of these unclean traits creep into us and corrupt our spiritual life, and so that we may uproot from our souls, one by one, every plant that our heavenly Father has not planted. The purification of the mother
The impurity of her infirmity: the days of a woman's monthly period.

Bearing children was a blessing and a divine command before the Fall. But after the Fall and the curse, bearing offspring became the bearing of sinful children who carry the sin of Adam and Eve. So childbirth was counted as an uncleanness, so that the woman might remember her sins and so that it might be an occasion for repentance. And because whatever she touches would be unclean, this calls her to complete rest, which helps her regain her health after the labors of childbirth. The woman who gives birth is unclean for seven days if she bears a male child.
Foreskin: a small piece of skin that is removed from the child's male organ.

The newborn is circumcised on the eighth day so that he may become a member of the people of God. His nature is renewed on the eighth day, which signifies eternity, where he receives a spiritual nature fit for the Kingdom. And because circumcision is a type of Baptism, which gives us new life in Christ and prepares us for the Kingdom of Heaven, it is no longer necessary to perform it in the New Testament, and when Christians do it, it is for health reasons only.
The sanctuary: the tabernacle of meeting.

The blood of her purifying: the blood that comes after childbirth. Blood is the basis of life, and its flowing points to the death that came upon man because of sin. So in the Old Testament it was considered an uncleanness and required a period of purification; but in the New Testament, through the death of Christ and the shedding of His blood, we receive cleansing from our sins, and the flow of blood is not considered an uncleanness. The woman remained in her uncleanness for the following thirty-three days, so that the whole period was forty days from the birth. She was not to touch anything holy or come to the house of the Lord. In the New Testament, Christ has lifted uncleanness from woman and from all His people by His salvation; yet she cannot partake of the Holy Mysteries, because of the lack of fitness and bodily cleanliness. The Law set forty days so that the effects of the flow of blood would end for all women, even those who take longer than others.

The period is doubled in the case of the birth of a female child, so that the mother may remember that the woman fell into sin before the man, tempted him, and afterward caused him to fall into sin. So the mother offers a doubled repentance for herself, not for the baby girl, so that she may live with God in depth and encourage her husband to the spiritual life.

Celebrate the feast of your Baptism at every baptism you attend, just as you celebrate your birthday, because Baptism is the beginning of your spiritual life, your sonship to God, and your worthiness to inherit eternal life. Remember that you have received a new nature, so that you may live to God in all your thoughts, words and deeds, and not to the world.
A lamb of the first year: one year old.
A young pigeon: a small dove.

We notice that the sacrifice is one and the same for the newborn, male or female, a sign of the equality of the two sexes in God's sight (Gal 3:28, Col 3:11). And the pairing of the burnt offering and the sin offering, which are the lamb and the young pigeon, shows the double work of Christ in:
1- Pleasing the Father (the burnt offering).
2- Paying the price of the sins of humanity (the sin offering).
The fountain of her blood: the blood that was flowing from the woman who had given birth.

Offering the burnt offering and the sin offering for the woman who has given birth cleanses her from the blood that was flowing from her after childbirth, and this is a type of the blood of Christ, which cleanses us in the sacraments of Baptism, confession and Communion. The blood that a woman sheds is a symbol of the death that came upon the human race because of sin. Death was considered an uncleanness, and whoever touched the dead became unclean; likewise blood was considered an uncleanness. But Christ by His blood took away our sins, so that the blood a woman sheds in the New Testament is not considered an uncleanness but a health ailment.

The poor could substitute a young dove or a young turtledove for the lamb of the burnt offering. This was the sacrifice of the Virgin Mary, who fulfilled the rite in spite of the purity of her childbirth, so that her humility and her fulfilling of the Law might be clear to us. The Virgin was a human being upon whom lay the sin of Adam and Eve, and she was not conceived without stain, so she needed purification through the sacrifices that signify the sacrifice of Christ her Savior. We notice that the sin offering is a turtledove or a young pigeon, a cheap bird, to take away the sin of the woman who has given birth; but the burnt offering is according to the financial means of the woman giving birth: either a lamb, or a turtledove, or a young pigeon.

Let us remember Him who became poor for our sake, though He is the source of all riches, so that we may thank Him abundantly, and so that all the material things of the world and their wealth may become small in our eyes. Then we shall not grow weary from material hardship, or bodily weakness, or any problems that pass over us, because our God is strong, and our Redeemer will deliver us from them all and comfort our hearts during these afflictions.
Leprosy of persons and of garments: introduction
Leprosy is a contagious skin disease that disfigures the body; it existed in the Old Testament.

Leprosy was connected with sin and might be a punishment for it, as in the case of Miriam the sister of Moses (Num 12:10-15), Gehazi the disciple of the prophet Elisha (2 Kgs 5:27), and King Uzziah (2 Chr 26:19-23). The priest would diagnose the disease and then confirm that it had gone, after the sick person had been separated for a period of time from mixing with the people. When he was healed of the disease, he offered sacrifices through the priest, and God forgave him his sins.
There was no cure for this disease, but healing comes from God. The healing is called cleansing, because it is deliverance from the effects of sin.
(a) Leprosy of persons (vv. 1-46). It includes various symptoms that reveal the presence of the disease, which are:

(1) White hair (vv. 1-3). 1 And the LORD spake unto Moses and Aaron, saying, 2 “When a man shall have in the skin of his flesh a rising, a scab, or bright spot, and it be in the skin of his flesh like the plague of leprosy; then he shall be brought unto Aaron the priest, or unto one of his sons the priests: 3 And the priest shall look on the plague in the skin of the flesh: and when the hair in the plague is turned white, and the plague in sight be deeper than the skin of his flesh, it is a plague of leprosy: and the priest shall look on him, and pronounce him unclean.”
The Lord spoke to Moses because he was the leader of the people, and to Aaron because he was the high priest, responsible with his sons for carrying out the Law.
A rising: a swelling, a tumor, or the mark of a wound.
A scab: a skin eruption.
A bright spot: a patch on the skin of a different color.

If a raised part, or a red or shining white part, was noticed on the skin of any Jewish person, they would bring him to the priest so that he might examine it and know whether these were signs of leprosy or of another skin disease.

The examination was held between the sixth hour and the ninth hour by Jewish reckoning, that is, from twelve to three in the afternoon, when the light of the sun is strong. The sick person's coming to the priest is a symbol of the sinner's turning to the father of confession to repent, so that the priest may examine his sins and guide him to the means of curing sin. The examination was not made on the Sabbath, because it is a day set apart for worship, so it was put off to the following day; and if the priest wished, he could seek the help of some experienced persons from among the people to diagnose the disease.

The priest examines him. If he finds in the discolored skin hair that has turned white, and also a depression in the skin, he is sure that it is the disease of leprosy, and he orders that the person be declared unclean and isolated.

If strange thoughts war against you and you doubt yourself, then turn to your father of confession and disclose your thoughts to him, and God will guide you through his tongue, so that you may resist the deceiving devil, repel the thoughts, and fortify yourself with the means of grace as your spiritual father guides you.

(2) The bright spot (vv. 4-8). 4 “If the bright spot be white in the skin of his flesh, and in sight be not deeper than the skin, and the hair thereof be not turned white; then the priest shall shut up him that hath the plague seven days: 5 And the priest shall look on him the seventh day: and, behold, if the plague in his sight be at a stay, and the plague spread not in the skin; then the priest shall shut him up seven days more: 6 And the priest shall look on him again the seventh day: and, behold, if the plague be somewhat dark, and the plague spread not in the skin, the priest shall pronounce him clean: it is but a scab: and he shall wash his clothes, and be clean. 7 But if the scab spread much abroad in the skin, after that he hath been seen of the priest for his cleansing, he shall be seen of the priest again: 8 And if the priest see that, behold, the scab spreadeth in the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean: it is a leprosy.”

The second symptom that the disease of leprosy may have is the appearance of a white spot in the skin, but without white hair in it and without a depression in the skin. This symptom may be leprosy or a similar skin disease, so the priest shuts him up with him for seven days, to make sure first whether the disease advances and other symptoms appear. The confinement was in tents near the tabernacle of meeting in the wilderness of Sinai, or in side rooms of the Temple in Jerusalem. The elders of the Jews did not shut up a suspected person on his wedding day or during the feasts of Unleavened Bread and Tabernacles.
In his sight: as the priest sees it.
If after seven days the priest notices that the white spot has not increased, he shuts him up for another seven days to be sure.
Dark: its color is deep.
Scab: a mark that is not harmful to the skin.

If after the second seven days the priest notices that the spot has not increased but its color has become darker, it is not leprosy; so he pronounces him clean, because this is merely a mark on the skin and not leprosy.
If after seven days the priest notices that the spots on the skin have increased, he shuts him up another seven days to make sure that it is the disease of leprosy.
If the priest notices that the spots on the skin have spread and increased, he judges that it is the disease of leprosy and orders the sick person to be isolated because of his uncleanness.

Do not be hasty in your judgments, lest you wrong another. Ask for God's guidance, think calmly, and seek counsel from the spiritual fathers as much as you can, especially in big decisions, and be confident that God will value your prayer and your turning to Him and will guide you to what is for your good and the good of others.

(3) White spots with raw flesh in them (vv. 9-11). 9 “When the plague of leprosy is in a man, then he shall be brought unto the priest; 10 And the priest shall see him: and, behold, if the rising be white in the skin, and it have turned the hair white, and there be quick raw flesh in the rising; 11 It is an old leprosy in the skin of his flesh, and the priest shall pronounce him unclean, and shall not shut him up: for he is unclean.”

The third case of leprosy is the presence of white spots higher than the ordinary skin, that is, a swelling, with white hair in it, but inside these white spots there are portions of living flesh, that is, the natural color of the body's flesh. In this case the priest judges that it is the disease of leprosy and isolates the sick person because of his uncleanness. This symptom declares that the disease of leprosy is of long standing in the sick person, that is, chronic, and so he is certainly unclean.

Do not be lenient with sin until it becomes deep in you and you grow accustomed to it, and you need greater striving to be rid of it. Cut off the sources of sin from the beginning and confess it, and you will be cleansed of it quickly with little striving.

The fourth case in the appearance of the disease of leprosy is the spreading of the white spots until they cover the whole body, that is, the whole skin becomes white. This means that the course of the disease is complete and the skin will return to its natural color, so the priest pronounces him clean. Spiritually, this signifies that the sick person has felt his complete lack, repented and humbled himself, and so deserves forgiveness and healing.

If the leprosy spreads and covers the whole body, but the priest discovers the presence of even small portions of living flesh, that is, the natural color of the body, among the white, he judges him leprous and unclean. Spiritually, this signifies wavering between a life of purity and uncleanness, or between good and evil.

In the last case mentioned in (vv. 14, 15), if the portions that were the color of living flesh change and become white, that is, the whole body becomes white, it is like the case mentioned in (vv. 12, 13), and he is pronounced clean.
Try to remain steadfast in your spiritual path and in carrying out your rule of prayer, so that you may abide in life with God and receive forgiveness, for the wavering person is unclean before God.
The case here arose as a mark in the skin after an abscess or boil that left a white sign tending to redness, or a raised mark, so he is brought to the priest.

The priest examines the sick person. If he finds in the mark of the boil a depression in the skin with white hair in it, he knows that it is the disease of leprosy and pronounces him unclean; that is, he finds in the place of the boil some parts raised in the skin and other parts depressed.

If by examination the priest finds that the place of the boil is a dark-colored spot, with no depression in the skin or white hair, he shuts him up seven days to be sure whether it is the disease of leprosy or not, because these signs are not sufficient to diagnose leprosy.
If the priest notices that the spot spreads in the skin, it is the disease of leprosy, and he pronounces the sick person unclean.
If the spot that is in the mark of the boil does not spread, it is merely a mark of it and not one of the symptoms of leprosy, so the priest pronounces him clean.

If you have repented of a sin, do not keep traces of it in your life, such as an evil friend, bad pictures, or any matters that had a connection with sin. Rather, get rid of all of it firmly, lest it bring you back to worse sins.
Keep away from the sources of sin and cling to the Church, and you will be steadfast in the life of repentance.

(6) A burning of fire (vv. 24-28). 24 “Or if there be any flesh, in the skin whereof there is a hot burning, and the quick flesh that burneth have a white bright spot, somewhat reddish, or white; 25 Then the priest shall look upon it: and, behold, if the hair in the bright spot be turned white, and it be in sight deeper than the skin; it is a leprosy broken out of the burning: wherefore the priest shall pronounce him unclean: it is the plague of leprosy. 26 But if the priest look on it, and, behold, there be no white hair in the bright spot, and it be no lower than the other skin, but be somewhat dark; then the priest shall shut him up seven days: 27 And the priest shall look upon him the seventh day: and if it be spread much abroad in the skin, then the priest shall pronounce him unclean: it is the plague of leprosy. 28 And if the bright spot stay in his place, and spread not in the skin, but it be somewhat dark; it is a rising of the burning, and the priest shall pronounce him clean: for it is an inflammation of the burning.”
"The quick flesh that burneth": the skin that has been renewed in the place of the burn.
Treatment by cauterizing was used anciently, but after the skin grows back in the place of the burn, its color may be white or white tending to redness.
This must be shown to the priest so that he may examine it for the three signs of leprosy explained above, which are:
a depression in the surface of the skin, whiteness of the hair, and spreading. If he finds them, he pronounces the sick person unclean.
There may remain only a mark of the burn of a color darker than the color of the skin, so the sick person is isolated for seven days so that the priest may be sure of his cleanness.
If the mark spreads, it was leprosy; but if it does not spread, it is merely a mark of the burn, which is harmless.

Pray much that God may remove the trace of the wars of lust from your heart, so that you do not desire your old sins lest you be burned by their fire once again. Resist evil thoughts by repeating prayers, however long the thoughts continue, and be confident that God rejoices in this striving of yours, for it is evidence of your repentance, and He upholds you until you are rid of them and come out of this war with a stronger spiritual will and spiritual growth.

(7) A plague on the head or beard (vv. 29-37). 29 “If a man or woman have a plague upon the head or the beard; 30 Then the priest shall see the plague: and, behold, if it be in sight deeper than the skin; and there be in it a yellow thin hair; then the priest shall pronounce him unclean: it is a dry scall, even a leprosy upon the head or beard. 31 And if the priest look on the plague of the scall, and, behold, it be not in sight deeper than the skin, and that there is no black hair in it; then the priest shall shut up him that hath the plague of the scall seven days: 32 And in the seventh day the priest shall look on the plague: and, behold, if the scall spread not, and there be in it no yellow hair, and the scall be not in sight deeper than the skin; 33 He shall be shaven, but the scall shall he not shave; and the priest shall shut up him that hath the scall seven days more: 34 And in the seventh day the priest shall look on the scall: and, behold, if the scall be not spread in the skin, nor in sight deeper than the skin; then the priest shall pronounce him clean: and he shall wash his clothes, and be clean. 35 But if the scall spread much in the skin after his cleansing; 36 Then the priest shall look on him: and, behold, if the scall be spread in the skin, the priest shall not seek for yellow hair; he is unclean. 37 But if the scall be in his sight at a stay, and that there is black hair grown up therein; the scall is healed, he is clean: and the priest shall pronounce him clean.”
Plague: an abnormal sign.

The skin disease may be in the head or beard of a man or a woman. As the Apostle Paul says that the head of the man is Christ, a plague in the head of a man signifies a weakness or defect that has afflicted his faith in Christ; but the head of the woman is the man, so a plague in the head of a woman signifies a defect in her relationship with her husband. As for the beard, it signifies dignity and honor, so a plague in it signifies the effect of sins in dishonoring a person's spiritual dignity.
Yellow: of a yellow color.

Thin: fine (weak). Scall: a scalp disease (a contagious skin disease). If the priest notices a depression of the skin and the presence of yellow hair, he pronounces the sick person unclean, because it is the disease of leprosy, which has appeared in the form of a scall on the head or beard.

If the priest notices that the skin is not depressed but the hair is not black and its color has changed, this means that some of the signs have disappeared, so isolation for seven days is called for, to be deliberate in judgment, and the lack of spreading is a sign that calls for further confirmation.

The priest shaves the place around the plague so that it appears clearly, and shuts up the sick person, isolated, for another seven days. If it is established that it has not spread, he is clean, and he washes his clothes as a confirmation of his cleanness.
But if the spots spread in the skin and the priest notices this after shutting him up seven days, it means that it is leprosy, and he pronounces him unclean even if he finds no yellow hair.

The sick person is not counted clean unless the spreading of the disease has stopped and black hair, that is, strong and sound hair, has reappeared. This signifies the person's return to his spiritual strength, and so he is clean.
Keep up the means of grace to be rid of every weakness that befalls you because of sin, and regular Communion is among the most important of these strengthening means.

(8) The freckled spot (vv. 38, 39). 38 “If a man also or a woman have in the skin of their flesh bright spots, even white bright spots; 39 Then the priest shall look: and, behold, if the bright spots in the skin of their flesh be darkish white; it is a freckled spot that groweth in the skin; he is clean.”
Bright spots, bright spots: patches, patches.
Freckled spot: this is the disease of vitiligo, which appears in the form of white patches on the skin, and it is not contagious.

If the priest finds a person with dark white patches on his skin, that is, not pure white, and there are no other signs in the skin, this is not leprosy but the disease of vitiligo, so he pronounces him clean.

Do not be hasty in judging people, for they may have an appearance that you think is connected with sin .. Be patient in judgment, for they may be pure, and do not busy yourself much with judging others, but look only for virtues, make excuses for mistakes, and pray for everyone, and for yourself before them.

(9) Baldness (vv. 40-44). 40 “And the man whose hair is fallen off his head, he is bald; yet is he clean. 41 And he that hath his hair fallen off from the part of his head toward his face, he is forehead bald: yet is he clean. 42 And if there be in the bald head, or bald forehead, a white reddish sore; it is a leprosy sprung up in his bald head, or his bald forehead. 43 Then the priest shall look upon it: and, behold, if the rising of the sore be white reddish in his bald head, or in his bald forehead, as the leprosy appeareth in the skin of the flesh; 44 He is a leprous man, he is unclean: the priest shall pronounce him utterly unclean; his plague is in his head.”
Bald: the falling out of all the hair of the head.
Forehead bald: the falling out of the hair from the front of the head only.
The condition here is not a disease, whether through the falling out of all the hair of the head or the hair from the front of the head only.
But the appearance of the symptoms of leprosy in the head establishes the person's uncleanness, and they are white spots tending to redness.

Having any lack in you in material respects, such as poverty or sickness, is no disgrace to you, provided it is not accompanied by any symptoms of sin, that is, the lack does not lead to grumbling, or resentment of others, or any bad treatment. Accept your inability and your weakness, do not compare yourself with anyone, and be confident that God will make you complete, and you will be in fullness and spiritual happiness.

(10) The law of the leper (vv. 45, 46). 45 “And the leper in whom the plague is, his clothes shall be rent, and his head bare, and he shall put a covering upon his upper lip, and shall cry, Unclean, unclean. 46 All the days wherein the plague shall be in him he shall be defiled; he is unclean: he shall dwell alone; without the camp shall his habitation be.”
The camp: the place where the people's tents were set up.
The leper is obliged to do five things once his infection with leprosy is established, which are:

1- He rends his clothes, and this signifies the exposure of sin, since the body of the one afflicted with the disease is shown; note that this applied to men only and not to women, out of regard for their modesty.
2- Baring the head, that is, not wearing a turban or the like, and this signifies his loss of dignity because of sin.
3- The man covering his upper lip, as a symbol of his loss of his spiritual manliness because of his weakness and his fall into sin.
4- He cries out about himself that he is unclean, and this means his confession of his sin, and also that no one may come near him and touch him and so make others unclean.
5- He is isolated from the place where people dwell, as a symbol of his loss of his communion in the Church.

All these duties help the sick person to repent and reject all his old sins, so that God may have compassion on him and heal him of his disease. Leprosy is a disease that indicates the uncleanness of man, and it has symptoms as already explained in this chapter. God allows this disease because of man's falling into great sins, and there is no healing from this disease by drugs or any medical treatment; healing comes from God, confirming that this disease is connected with sin and its cure is repentance.

Take care to confess your sins and humble yourself before God, and do not be angry if your father of confession gives you a discipline such as deprivation from Communion, for all this helps you to repent, so that you receive God's mercies and regain your spiritual strength.

(b) Leprosy of garments (vv. 47-59). 47 “The garment also that the plague of leprosy is in, whether it be a woollen garment, or a linen garment; 48 Whether it be in the warp, or woof; of linen, or of woollen; whether in a skin, or in any thing made of skin; 49 And if the plague be greenish or reddish in the garment, or in the skin, either in the warp, or in the woof, or in any thing of skin; it is a plague of leprosy, and shall be shewed unto the priest: 50 And the priest shall look upon the plague, and shut up it that hath the plague seven days: 51 And he shall look on the plague on the seventh day: if the plague be spread in the garment, either in the warp, or in the woof, or in a skin, or in any work that is made of skin; the plague is a fretting leprosy; it is unclean. 52 He shall therefore burn that garment, whether warp or woof, in woollen or in linen, or any thing of skin, wherein the plague is: for it is a fretting leprosy; it shall be burnt in the fire. 53 And if the priest shall look, and, behold, the plague be not spread in the garment, either in the warp, or in the woof, or in any thing of skin; 54 Then the priest shall command that they wash the thing wherein the plague is, and he shall shut it up seven days more: 55 And the priest shall look on the plague, after that it is washed: and, behold, if the plague have not changed his colour, and the plague be not spread; it is unclean; thou shalt burn it in the fire; it is fret inward, whether it be bare within or without. 56 And if the priest look, and, behold, the plague be somewhat dark after the washing of it; then he shall rend it out of the garment, or out of the skin, or out of the warp, or out of the woof: 57 And if it appear still in the garment, either in the warp, or in the woof, or in any thing of skin; it is a spreading plague: thou shalt burn that wherein the plague is with fire. 58 And the garment, either warp, or woof, or whatsoever thing of skin it be, which thou shalt wash, if the plague be departed from them, then it shall be washed the second time, and shall be clean. 59 This is the law of the plague of leprosy in a garment of woollen or linen, either in the warp, or woof, or any thing of skins, to pronounce it clean, or to pronounce it unclean.”
Garments too may be infected with leprosy. A person's clothes signify his conduct, so it must be pure in his appearance, his speech and his behavior.
Warp: the lengthwise threads of the fabric.
Woof: the crosswise threads of the fabric.

The spot carrying the infection may appear in the lengthwise or crosswise threads of the fabric of the garment, whether wool or linen, and it appears also in the garment or article of skin, and its color tends to greenish or reddish. Then the garment is shown to the priest.
The priest examines the garments. If he finds in them the symptoms mentioned above, he isolates them for seven days; and if the plague spreads, the garment is leprous and unclean.
The priest burns the garment because it is unclean and to prevent the spread of infection, and this signifies cutting off sin and keeping away from it completely, whatever the loss.
Any thing: that is, articles made of skin.
If the plague has not spread, the priest has it washed and isolates the garment for another week.
Fret: a hole or erosion.
Bare: the worn place in the cloth.

If the plague has not spread but its appearance remains as it was and has not disappeared with washing, and this is clear after the garment has dried, the garment is considered unclean and must be burned. The infection will have caused a hole or erosion, whether on the inside of the garment or the outside. This signifies the need for continued repentance in order to cut off any traces of sin.

But if the color of the infection remains dark after washing, the priest tears out only the area of the plague, out of care not to spoil and lose the whole garment; but it is torn out lest it turn into leprosy afterward. This signifies being on guard against what leads to sin and keeping away from it.
Spreading: living leprosy that breeds and increases.
If the infection reappears in the garment, it is then of the living kind that can spread, so the whole garment is burned.

But if the plague disappears after washing, it was merely a spot, so the garment is washed again to confirm its cleanness and then used again because it is clean. Thus one must guard against every appearance of evil.
Such is the law concerning the leprosy of garments.

Would that you were careful about your conduct and appearance, and even about every word you utter and every word you hear, lest by hearing it repeatedly it makes you fall into sin. And do not forget that you will give an account on the Day of Judgment for every idle word. In this way you keep yourself pure from every evil and every appearance of evil.
The cleansing of the leper and leprosy of houses: introduction

To show the hideousness of sin so that man may hate it, the leper is isolated, because his disease signifies uncleanness, and he stays outside the camp, away from the people, until he repents, and then God heals him, since he has no medical cure. Then he needs three stages for his cleansing, so that he may feel the importance of the new, pure life that he will receive, hold fast to it and keep away from every sin. These steps of cleansing signify the redemption that Christ accomplished on the Cross and gave us in the Church and her sacraments.
(a) The cleansing of the leper (vv. 1-20). It includes three stages, which are:

God declared to Moses, the leader of the people, the rite for the cleansing of the leper. It begins with one of the acquaintances or family of the leper telling the priest that he has been healed, and bringing him to the priest outside the camp. The family of the leper signifies the Church, which brings sinners to Christ, the Great High Priest, to cleanse them from all their sins.

The priest goes out to the leper outside the camp, where his family has brought him to him. The going out of the priest signifies the Incarnation of Christ and His going out outside the camp to die for our sins; it is He who drew near to us to redeem and cleanse us.
The priest examines the leper, and if he finds that the leprosy has left his skin, he begins the rite of cleansing with him.

May we care for sinners and those who are far away, offering them love and encouraging them to be joined to the Church, and may we make the priests aware of their circumstances so that they may care for them. Just as the four carried their paralyzed friend, let us carry our brethren to Christ, so that they may find healing from all their troubles and may be established and rejoice in the Church.
Two birds ... clean: in some translations, two clean fowls; the meaning is two clean birds or two clean sparrows, because sparrows are among the clean birds.
Cedar wood: a piece of wood from the tall cedar trees that are abundant in Palestine and Lebanon. Scarlet: a piece of cloth of a dark red color.
Hyssop: a small, weak plant with small leaves, resembling the parsley plant.

The leper is cleansed on the first day by bringing two birds, which either the rich or the poor can bring because they are cheap. Birds signify loftiness because they fly toward heaven, like the loftiness of Christ the Redeemer and the loftiness that the leper should display in his new life.
They also bring a piece of cedar wood, which signifies the wood of the Cross, and also loftiness, because of the height of cedar trees.
Likewise a piece of scarlet cloth, which signifies the blood of Christ the Redeemer.
And also a bunch of the delicate little hyssop plant, which signifies the humility that appeared in Christ and that the leper should display in order to be cleansed.

Running water: flowing water like the water of rivers, not stagnant water like that of marshes. The bird is killed over it because the blood of a bird is little, so by mixing it with the water, the things that will be mentioned in (v. 6) can be dipped in it. The priest kills one of the birds outside the camp, far from the tabernacle of the congregation and the bronze altar, for the two birds offered are not among the known sacrifices offered on the bronze altar; rather, this is a special law for the cleansing of the leper.
The killing is done in an earthen vessel filled with running water, so that the blood of the bird, which is little, falls on this water.

The earthen vessel signifies the divine Incarnation, the water signifies the work of the Holy Spirit and the sacrament of Baptism, and the slain bird signifies Christ the Redeemer crucified on the Cross.

The priest takes the second bird, which is still alive, together with the piece of cedar wood, the scarlet and the hyssop plants. He may bind them together, or hold the three together in his hand, and dips them in the blood of the bird mixed with the running water, because the living bird signifies the risen Christ, yet bearing the marks of the wounds that were inflicted on the Cross, as the Book of Revelation mentions (Rev 5:6).

He sprinkles the water mixed with blood, in which the hyssop, the scarlet and the living bird were dipped, on the leper seven times. This signifies the fullness of the cleansing, because the number "7" signifies the week, that is, the fullness of life, so that the cleansed leper lives a new life with God all his days. It also signifies the Holy Spirit, who gives complete purity, as He cleanses us through the seven sacraments of the Church. Then the priest lets the living bird go, directing it toward the wilderness. This signifies the risen Christ, as we said, who rose to raise us up, we who live in the wilderness of the world, and to lift us up to the heavens.

After this the leper takes steps to complete his cleansing. This shows the importance of spiritual striving alongside the work of divine grace that is accomplished by Christ the Redeemer. These steps are:
1- The leper washes his clothes, as a symbol of the purity of the conduct he will live after his healing from the disease.
2- He shaves off all his hair, as a sign of ridding himself of all sins through repentance.
3- He bathes in water, which signifies the two sacraments of Baptism and confession.

4- The leper stays inside the camp, but not in his tent; rather, in a special place for seven days, as a symbol of the importance of the sojourn in the world in which the cleansed leper should live, that is, that he should not be absorbed in material desires lest he fall again into one of the sins. The number "7" signifies the fullness of life, that is, that he should live all his life without attachment to material things.

Repentance is not a word you say; rather, it is steps you must pass through: keeping away from the sources of sin, clinging to the Church, practicing the sacraments of confession and Holy Communion, and then living in asceticism, using the world but without being absorbed in it.
Of the first year: one year old.
Three tenth deals: about 7 liters.
A log: 1/3 of a liter.

On the eighth day of the cleansing of the leper he offers sacrifices and offerings. The eighth day signifies eternity, that is, that he lives pure all his life, and then this extends forever in heaven.

It is noted that the leper now offers the sacrifices and offerings himself for the first time after his healing, because he has entered the camp. This signifies the importance of spiritual striving as long as a person is able to carry out the practices of spiritual striving, such as fasting and prostrations (metanoias) ...
The cleansed man brings four kinds of offerings, which are:

1- A lamb for the trespass offering, which must be sound, that is, without blemish, because Christ our Redeemer is without blemish. He offers a trespass offering because he may have sinned against God and His laws or wronged others; these wrongs are also directed against God, in addition to his failure in worship and in offering the sacrifices at the feasts, because he was sick and isolated outside the camp.

2- A ewe as a sin offering, for the sins he committed that caused him this disease. He offers a ewe, that is, a female, because the female gives birth and yields offspring, that is, fruits; this signifies the removal of sins and all their fruits and the beginning of the new life with its spiritual fruits.

3- A second lamb for the burnt offering, so that God may be pleased with the sick man, from whom, because of his sin, the face of God was hidden, and may be pleased with him through this burnt offering, which signifies Christ, through whom we were reconciled with heaven.
4- A grain offering, which includes:

a- Three tenths of fine flour; one tenth is offered with each of the trespass offering, the sin offering and the burnt offering. These signify the pure life of Christ that He lived on earth, and point to the new, pure life in which the healed sick man wants to live with God.

b- A log of oil, which is pure olive oil, used in the offerings presented to God because of its purity; it signifies the work of the Holy Spirit, who will work in this healed sick man in his new life.

The priest in charge of the cleansing of the leper brings the healed sick man who stands before God to be cleansed, and places in his hands the slaughtered lamb to offer as a trespass offering, and the log of oil with one tenth of the flour mingled with oil, and waves them before God. That is, he moves his hands forward and backward, to the right and to the left, offering them to God who fills every place and is present in the four directions; and he lifts his hands up and then down, that is, he offers them to God who dwells in heaven, and lowers them down, that is, offered on his behalf.

The trespass offering is slaughtered, like the sin offering and the burnt offering, before the bronze altar at the entrance of the tabernacle of the congregation. The one who offers it does not eat of it; rather, he offers a part to God and the rest to the priest, that is, it is all holy to God and His priest. With it he offers one tenth of the flour, according to the rite of the grain offering mentioned in (ch. 2).

The Jewish scholars say that two priests performed this service. One of them gathers the blood in a basin and sprinkles it around the altar, according to the rite of the sacrifice mentioned in (ch. 5), while the other priest takes some of the blood and anoints the tip of the ear of the one offering the sacrifice, as a symbol of the sanctification of his hearing, that is, that he should take care to listen to pure conversations; then he anoints with the blood the thumb of his right hand, as a symbol of the sanctification of his works, because the right hand represents strength and the thumb is the most important finger. Then he anoints the great toe of his right foot, as a symbol of the sanctification of his conduct, that is, that he should walk in the way of God. Of course, one priest can perform this service, gathering the blood and then anointing the one offering the sacrifice.

The priest takes the log of oil, that is, the vessel in which the oil is, and pours it into his left hand. Then with the finger of his right hand he sprinkles some of this oil seven times toward the bronze altar and the sanctuary, that is, he presents the work of the Holy Spirit, who is signified by the number "7", before God to cleanse the sick man.

The priest takes some of the remaining oil in his left hand and anoints the right ear of the cleansed man, the thumb of his right hand and the great toe of his right foot, on top of the blood with which they were anointed before, as a symbol of the sanctification by the Holy Spirit of what he hears, what he does and the way he walks.
The priest pours the rest of the oil in his left hand on the head of the cleansed man, and this signifies the cleansing of his thoughts.

The priest offers the ewe, the sin offering for the cleansed man, and with it one tenth of the flour mingled with oil, by the same rite mentioned in (ch. 4); then he offers the lamb of the burnt offering, and with it one tenth of the flour mingled with oil, by the same rite mentioned in (ch. 1). Thus is completed the cleansing of the leper whom God healed.

So that you may live pure, take care to keep your eyes away from unclean sights, direct your hearing to pure words, and be careful in your works and conduct. And when God sees your care, He fills you with His love, and you feel Him in your life and rejoice with Him.
(b) The cleansing of the poor leper (vv. 21-32):

21 "And if he be poor, and cannot get so much; then he shall take one lamb for a trespass offering to be waved, to make an atonement for him, and one tenth deal of fine flour mingled with oil for a meat offering, and a log of oil; 22 And two turtledoves, or two young pigeons, such as he is able to get; and the one shall be a sin offering, and the other a burnt offering. 23 And he shall bring them on the eighth day for his cleansing unto the priest, unto the door of the tabernacle of the congregation, before the LORD. 24 And the priest shall take the lamb of the trespass offering, and the log of oil, and the priest shall wave them for a wave offering before the LORD: 25 And he shall kill the lamb of the trespass offering, and the priest shall take some of the blood of the trespass offering, and put it upon the tip of the right ear of him that is to be cleansed, and upon the thumb of his right hand, and upon the great toe of his right foot: 26 And the priest shall pour of the oil into the palm of his own left hand: 27 And the priest shall sprinkle with his right finger some of the oil that is in his left hand seven times before the LORD: 28 And the priest shall put of the oil that is in his hand upon the tip of the right ear of him that is to be cleansed, and upon the thumb of his right hand, and upon the great toe of his right foot, upon the place of the blood of the trespass offering: 29 And the rest of the oil that is in the priest's hand he shall put upon the head of him that is to be cleansed, to make an atonement for him before the LORD. 30 And he shall offer the one of the turtledoves, or of the young pigeons, such as he can get; 31 Even such as he is able to get, the one for a sin offering, and the other for a burnt offering, with the meat offering: and the priest shall make an atonement for him that is to be cleansed before the LORD. 32 This is the law of him in whom is the plague of leprosy, whose hand is not able to get that which pertaineth to his cleansing." The place of the trespass offering (v. 28): the right ear, the thumb of the right hand and the great toe of the right foot, anointed with the blood.

God's mercy appears in not burdening the poor who were struck with leprosy and healed by God: they offer sacrifices and offerings of lesser cost, yet through them obtain complete cleansing. The difference between the offering of the poor man and that of the ordinary or rich person lies in two things:

The symptoms that give rise to suspicion of the disease of leprosy are defined by the Law in two appearances:
1- A patch inclining to greenish or reddish.
2- A depression in the wall or hollows in it.
If the priest notices the preceding symptoms, he suspects that it is leprosy, but in order to be sure of it he shuts up the house for seven days.

If after seven days the priest notices that the depressed patch has spread in the walls of the house, he suspects that it is leprosy, but it may be limited to a certain area, so he commands the following:
1- Taking out the stones in this area where the patch is and casting them outside the city in an unclean place, that is, not the place where the holy ashes of the sacrifices are cast.
2- Scraping the wall around these stones, gathering this dust and casting it also outside the city in an unclean place.

3- They put new stones in place of the first ones, and put on them the dust mixed with water that holds the stones fast, like the mortar used today, and they also coat the stones with clay to fill the cracks. This signifies keeping away from evil and everything connected with it.

If anyone enters, for any reason, a house suspected of being struck with leprosy which the priest has shut up for seven days, the one who entered against the priest's orders becomes unclean, even if he entered for only one minute, and remains unclean until the evening, and then he bathes and is clean.

This signifies calling oneself to account through repentance for every carelessness.
If the suspicion of leprosy has been treated by putting in new stones and dust, and no symptoms of leprosy appear afterward, the priest judges the house to be clean.

After the affected stones and the dust around them have been changed and the priest has judged that the house is healed of leprosy, the rite of cleansing is performed for the house. It is the same rite performed for the leper on the first day, which was explained earlier in (vv. 1-7) of this chapter.
Here he states that what was mentioned in this chapter and the preceding chapter are the laws of the disease of leprosy in its various forms.
