Oil, the showbread and blasphemy
Beaten: Oil is extracted from olives by beating or pounding them in a mortar, and the purest kind of oil comes out of them.

God commanded Moses to call the people to bring the oil with which the lamp in the Holy Place is kindled, not here only but previously in (Ex 25:6, 27:20, 21). With this oil the lamps are kindled by day and by night, on all the days. The oil is a symbol of the work of the Holy Spirit in the prophets and the men of God in the Old Testament and in all believers, that they may live with God and await the Messiah, the Savior.

The people's bringing of the oil is a blessing to them, because by it they share in offering the worship of God. Although only the priests enter the Holy Place, the people also enter through their gifts, which show their love for God and gladden His heart.

The veil of the testimony: The curtain that separates the Holy Place from the Holy of Holies, where the Ark of the Covenant is, and inside it the two tablets of the commandments, which bear witness to the existence of God and declare His commands to His people. Therefore it was called the Ark of the Testimony and the veil of the testimony.
Aaron: What is meant is Aaron and his sons, that is, the priests.

God continues His speech about the use of the oil in kindling the lamps of the lampstand that is in the Holy Place before the veil, and the priests take care to put in the oil and to kindle the lamps of the lampstand throughout the night and the day. He calls it the pure lampstand because everything in the Holy Place is pure and sanctified by blood. The priests also take care to clean the lampstand, so that it may be in purity and in an appearance worthy of God. The seven lamps of the lampstand are a symbol of the work of the Holy Spirit, as we mentioned in the Book of Exodus.

Offer some of your gifts to the Church and to the ministry, that you may receive the blessing of sharing in drawing souls to Christ. God does not forget your labor, even if it is a cup of cold water, and He will reward you for it in heaven, in addition to blessings in your life and your sense of God's support and companionship.

Here he speaks of the showbread that is placed on a table inside the Holy Place, whose details were explained before in (Ex 25). They make twelve cakes, each cake made of flour amounting to two tenths of an ephah, that is, about 4.6 liters. The number (12) means the twelve tribes, that is, this bread is offered on behalf of all the children of Israel before God continually. This means that God's eye is on the offerings of His children and on their lives, because God cares for them and rejoices in their offerings. The Levites ground the flour and purified it through twelve sieves, so that it would be easy to knead and without any impurities, that is, without blemish. It is made unleavened, that is, without yeast, because yeast is a symbol of evil and so is not offered before God.
The twelve cakes were placed on the table in two rows, six of them on top of one another in each. Each cake was large, measuring about 50 × 50 cm, while the table measured 50 × 100 cm.

Frankincense was placed on the showbread and remained there for a week, then it was burned before God as a fragrance of incense. This means that the bread is offered to receive God's blessing and the frankincense to please Him, a declaration by the people that they believe in God and worship Him and hope for His good pleasure and His blessing. The frankincense was usually placed in two golden dishes, and each dish was placed on a row of the rows of bread. The number (2) is a symbol of love, that is, the people's love for God.

The flour that the people of Israel offered to God was baked by the priests and the Levites, who renewed it every Sabbath on the table of the showbread. It remained on the table for seven days, then the new bread was put in its place, and they took the old bread out of the Holy Place, together with the frankincense that was on it. This renewal is a symbol of the people's continual love for God and the renewal of their covenants and their love for Him.

When they took the bread out of the Holy Place, they burned the frankincense that was on it before God, then the priests ate the bread in a holy place, that is, in the house of the Lord and the places attached to it. The priests' eating of it declares that there is a special blessing that God gives to His priests, which was fulfilled in the New Testament by the work of the Holy Spirit in the sacrament of the priesthood. The making of the showbread continued throughout the life of the children of Israel and their worship of God until Christ came.

God gives a special grace to the one who serves Him, so do not be hindered from serving God because of your weakness, for His power will work in you and fill you, so that you may give to others and draw them to God.

An Israelite woman of the tribe of Dan, called Shelomith, married an Egyptian man, most likely in the days of their stay in Egypt. When they left Egypt she lived outside the camp, because her husband was not one of the children of Israel. She bore a son, and this son quarreled with an Israelite man and fought with him. It seems that he was trying to dwell with the children of Israel, and this Israelite man prevented him. Then the Egyptian's son became angry and cursed the name of God, Jehovah, which the Jews held in great reverence. So the children of Israel rose up against this blasphemer, seized him and brought him to Moses, for him to decide what they should do with him for his insolence against the name of God.
Moses commanded that this man be put in custody temporarily, then he went to pray in the tabernacle of meeting and to seek God's guidance.

May you take refuge in God through prayer in all the matters of your life, and trust that He is able to speak to you in simple and easy ways, as long as you are concerned to hear Him. Thus you enjoy fellowship with God, and He leads your life in the straight way, and you succeed in all your affairs.

The Lord spoke to Moses and commanded him to bring the blasphemer outside the camp, where the tents of the children of Israel were, because the camp is sanctified by the presence of God and His people in it. For this reason they used to cast the ashes of the animals sanctified as sin offerings outside the camp, and the leper too lived outside the camp, for it represented the unclean place. For this reason also Christ was crucified outside the camp, that is, outside Jerusalem, bearing our reproach and our uncleanness. He also commanded that the witnesses who heard his blasphemy lay their hands on the head of the blasphemer, as a declaration of their testimony to his blasphemy and likewise a declaration that his blood is upon his own head. Then after that they stone him with stones until he dies, the witnesses beginning to stone him and then the rest of the people through the elders of the tribes or their delegates, because whoever is insolent against God has been insolent against all principles and commandments, and he cannot live in the midst of the congregation of God.
The stranger: One whose origin is not Jewish and who then joined the people of God, or who is a non-Jew.
He that is born in the land: that is, the Jew.

God gave Moses a commandment for all their lives, namely that whoever is insolent against God and reviles Him or speaks evil words against Him must die by stoning with stones, as a declaration of the horror of this sin, and all who dwell in the camp, Jews and non-Jews, take part in stoning him, so that all may learn respect for God and reverence for Him.

God feared for His people lest they make light of the lives of their brothers when He permitted the killing of one who blasphemes God, or lest one of them be enraged when another reviles him and try to kill him. So He warned them that no one should dare to kill another, for the sixth commandment forbids killing (Ex 20:13), and He confirms it here by saying that whoever kills anyone must be put to death, showing the importance of the human soul and its great value in God's sight.

God also stresses not wronging animals that others own, so that no one is enraged if an animal belonging to its owner harms him and rises and kills it. In this case he must compensate him with an animal like it, as He had already declared in (Ex 21).

Here He also confirms what He had already mentioned in (Ex 21), that it is not only a person's life that is precious in God's sight but any member of his body. If a man is enraged and wrongs his neighbor, so that harm befalls one of his members, then the wrongdoer must be harmed with the same harm that befell the victim. This is in order to keep them from wronging others and to prepare them for the idea of redemption, which He would accomplish in the fullness of time by the death of Christ as a redemption for mankind.

The elders of the Jews used to allow the wrongdoer to compensate for the harm by paying a sum determined by the judges, relying on the commands of the Law (Ex 21:30). What is meant by this commandment is not that the victim take revenge on the one who wronged him, but what we have mentioned, namely that a person should fear to wrong another and should be concerned for the life of his neighbor and all the members of his body.
Here He repeats the greatness of human life: whoever kills another must be put to death, but for a beast he makes restitution.
I am the Lord your God: that is, the just God.
God declares His justice, so that this law is applied to the Jew or to the non-Jew who dwells among them.

Moses carried out the word of God, so they brought out the son of Shelomith who had blasphemed God and stoned him outside the camp. Here the result of marriage with unbelievers appears, which is the begetting of a son who reviles God and is put to death by stoning.

Be careful lest by your conduct and your words you blaspheme the name of God, that is, lest you become a bad image that makes people insolent against the name of Christ and the Church. So be diligent, knowing that God is before you and sees all your deeds always, that you may fear Him and do what pleases Him.
The seventh year, the jubilee and the redemption
Shall keep a sabbath: The seventh year for the land, just as the Sabbath day is the seventh among the days of the week.

God continues His speech to Moses from between the two cherubim on the mercy seat of the Ark of the Covenant in the Holy of Holies in the tabernacle of meeting. He commands them a commandment that would be carried out after their entry into the land of Canaan and their cultivation of the land, which is that they cultivate the land for six years, but in the seventh year the land rests and they do not sow it. This has purposes, which are:
1- In this year they devote themselves to the worship of God, increasing their prayers and their readings in the holy books. At the Feast of Tabernacles in the seventh year they read the whole Law.
2- God's mercy toward His people appears, as He gives them rest from work in the seventh year, and likewise to the servants and the workers they employ.
3- The land rests from cultivation, and this renews its vigor and strength in the following years.
4- The crops that appear in the seventh year, or the fruits that come forth on the trees, are food for the owners of the land, for the poor and for the animals.

5- It strengthens the people's faith in God, because He promised them to give them a double yield in the sixth year, so that it would suffice for two years, since there is no harvest in the seventh year, which is not sown.
6- In this year the land that was sold returns to its owners, and the servants are also set free.
Gather in the fruit of your vineyard: Gather the clusters of grapes.
God permits the Jews to sow their lands with various crops and to reap them, and likewise to gather the fruits of their lands planted with trees, such as grapes, for six years.

The seventh year is to be a holiday and a rest for the land and for them. It began either after the Feast of Pentecost, when the winter crops are gathered, or after the Feast of Tabernacles, when the summer crops and the fruit of the trees are also gathered.

It is likely that the celebration of the seventh year did not begin seven years after their entry into the land of Canaan, because they spent the first seven years in wars to possess the land, and most likely they needed another seven years in which Joshua divided the land among them. Then they sowed the land for six years and celebrated in the twenty-first year from their entry into the Promised Land.
That which groweth of its own accord of thy harvest: The plants that spring up from the seeds that fell on the ground from the previous harvest.
Undressed: The grapes that the grape gatherers leave on the vines.

He forbids him to do any agricultural work in the seventh year, such as gathering the crops of plants that sprang up without care from him, from the seeds that fell during the harvest, or the shoots that grow at the base of the trees. Nor does he gather what remains on the trees of the fruits that the gatherers forgot, but he, together with the poor, may eat of them.

The plants that grow of themselves in the seventh year, or what remains of the fruits on the trees from the sixth year, are eaten by the owners of the land, the servants and the poor, and likewise the animals as well.

Be tender toward all who are around you. If God has compassion on the land, man, animals and plants, may you be like Him, having compassion on everyone and giving them their rest and their reward, especially those who suffer from harassment.
Seven sabbaths of years: Seven times the seventh year.
God commanded them to count seven times the seventh year, that is, (7 × 7), so that the total is 49 years, so that after it they might celebrate the fiftieth year, that is, the year of jubilee.

After 49 years have passed, on the Day of Atonement, that is, on the tenth day of the seventh month, they blow the trumpets throughout the land of the Jews, announcing the beginning of the fiftieth year, that is, the year of jubilee.
Jubilee: It means a trumpet, and what is meant is the fiftieth year, in which the trumpet is blown in all the land.
The Law declares what is done in the fiftieth year, which is:
1- The freeing and emancipation of the servants and the cancellation of the debts of the debtors.

2- The lands that were sold by their owners because of poverty are redeemed in it, so they return to their owners, to possess them and use them as they wish, that is, every person returns to dwell among his clan.
3- The year of jubilee is a year of rest for the land: they do not sow in it, nor reap, nor gather the rest of the fruits of the trees, such as grapes.

They devote themselves to worship and joy in the year of jubilee. Although they do not gather the plants that grow of themselves in the land, they may eat of them, they and the poor, and likewise the animals.
Every person who sold his land because of poverty recovers this land, and returns to the land that he possessed from his fathers. This is beneficial in the following respects:

1- Concern for the Promised Land, which is a symbol of the heavenly Jerusalem, that is, holding fast to the inheritance from the fathers, which is a symbol of the eternal inheritance. Even if he left it because of poverty and distress, in the year of jubilee, which is a symbol of the salvation that Christ accomplished on the cross, he regains the right to the eternal inheritance.
2- The rich are not preoccupied with seizing lands, that is, a limit is set within them to the love of money and possessions.
3- Mercy and compassion toward the poor who were compelled to sell their lands.
4- It teaches everyone that God is the giver of the land and that they are strangers in it, so that they may cling to heaven.
Oppress: Wrong.

In the year of jubilee each one reviews himself concerning the sales and purchases that took place earlier in his life. If he wronged someone and sold to him at a markup of less than a sixth of the price of the thing, he returns the difference to him, and if the markup was more than a sixth of the thing, this commercial transaction is annulled, because the measure of wrong in it is great. This is the interpretation of the elders of the Jews. The conclusion is that in the year of jubilee, which is a symbol of the mercy of Christ the Savior, each person reviews himself, whether he dealt mercifully with those around him or wronged himself, so as to correct this wrong.

The price of the land was estimated according to its nearness to the year of jubilee, because it is returned to its owner in that year. So if someone bought land a few years before the jubilee, its price would be cheap, and the opposite is true. The Law says in this verse "according to the years of the fruits," that is, what they reap from the land, because the one who buys is buying the right to benefit from the land and use it for a period of time, not the land itself, since it remains the property of its owner, because it is an inheritance from the fathers (v. 23). And it says "according unto the number of years of the fruits he shall sell unto thee," that is, he buys the crops of the years that precede the jubilee. If they are few, the price of the land is small, and if the years before the jubilee are many, the price of the land is great.
He stresses that no one should wrong another, declaring that He is the Lord their God, that is, the Just One who looks upon everything and will repay each one according to his works.
God promises them, if they obey this His law, that He will reward them with two things:
1- They will live in peace of heart, and He will protect them from their enemies, so that they are secure.
2- He will bless the land, so that it gives them abundant crops that satisfy their needs.

God used to bless the yield of the sixth year so that it would be double, because they do not sow in the seventh year. But in the year of jubilee they do not sow either, and before it comes a seventh year in which they do not sow, so that there are two years without cultivation of the land, the forty-ninth year and the fiftieth year. But God blesses the forty-eighth year, so that it yields three times as much, to suffice for the needs of the people for three years.

Whatever circumstances you meet or expect to meet, trust that the blessing of God, in whom you trust, will suffice for your needs, will face all the problems for you and will protect you from all troubles.

He affirms that the yield of the sixth year will suffice for the seventh and the eighth year until the yield of the eighth year comes, so that they eat of the old crop, that is, the former one, until they reap the new crop. This is the case with every seventh year. But in the year of jubilee, as we mentioned, the yield is three times as much, so that it suffices for the forty-ninth and the fiftieth year until the yield of the fifty-first year comes.

The land is God's property, and Joshua the son of Nun divided it among the tribes, so each one took his portion from God. It is therefore not permissible to sell the lands, because they are God's property; only the right to use them, that is, to take their crops, is sold, and that for a fixed period, then they return to their owner. God's ownership of the land makes His people feel that they are strangers in the world and that their true homeland is heaven. It also assures them of God's ownership of their lives and their lands, and that they are stewards over them, so that they may be faithful in using them and thank God at all times for granting them this land that they use and eat from. It also establishes a spirit of humility within them.

If a Jewish person became poor and sold his land, that is, someone bought from him the right to use it for a fixed period, then his nearest relative can pay its price to the one who bought it and redeem the land, so that it returns to its owner. And if he does not have the money with which to redeem his land and recover it for himself, then it is naturally redeemed and returns to him in the year of jubilee.
Kinsman: The nearest relative.
That which was sold: The land that was sold.

The kinsman had to care for his poor relative who sold his land, paying its price to the buyer and returning it to him. The Law here shows the importance of works of mercy and the responsibility of a relative for his needy relatives.

Care for your relatives and their spiritual and material needs, trying to encourage them to be attached to the Church and helping them in all their needs, for this is your responsibility before God. In this we feel in the Church that we are members of one body, the Body of Christ, trusting in the blessing of God that floods your life.

If the poor man who sold his land is able to gather an amount of money with which he can redeem his land and recover it, he counts the years in which the buyer used it and deducts them from the price for which he bought it, and pays him the rest, and so he redeems his land.

If he is unable to gather enough money to redeem his land and finds no kinsman to redeem the land for him, he waits patiently until the year of jubilee comes, and his land is redeemed and he recovers it, because all the lands are returned to their owners in that year. It is a symbol of Christ, who pays our debts and restores to us our sonship and our eternal inheritance after He paid the price of sin for us, which is death on the cross.

The condition of houses differs from that of the lands, which are God's property. The houses they built themselves, so they are their property and can be sold and are not recovered. But if a person became poor and sold his house, the mercy of the Law appears in that it gives him a year of opportunity to gather the required money and pay it to the buyer, and so recover his house, because he may have passed through special circumstances which he can overcome after a short time.

And if the buyer died, the price can be paid to his heir and the house recovered from him. And if the buyer traveled and did not return before a year from the sale, the seller can pay the price before the elders of Israel who are responsible for carrying out the Law, and recover his house.
Forever: Absolutely.
Throughout his generations: For his life and the life of his sons, for it is an inheritance for his children.
Shall not go out: Does not return to its owner.

If the seller does not recover his house within a year, it becomes the permanent property of its buyer and his heirs and does not return to the owner of the house in the year of jubilee, because houses, as we mentioned, are not like the lands, which are God's property, but are the property of their owners, who may sell and buy them.

As for the houses of the villages, they are weak buildings tied to the land, since the owner of the land lives in them to cultivate his fields. If they are sold, and most likely they are sold with the land so that the buyer and his workers may live in them and use the land in cultivating and reaping it, then when the year of jubilee comes the seller recovers his land and the houses that are on it.

As for the houses of the Levites that are inside their cities, if one of them sold, it returns to him in the year of jubilee, because they are consecrated to the service of God and have no fields or private occupations, so their houses must return to them. The owner of the land that he sold can arrange its price and pay it to the buyer at any time, before or after a year, to recover his house, and if he cannot, one of the Levites can redeem the land for him, and no member of another tribe is permitted to redeem the land for him. And if its owner or one of his relatives from the Levites does not redeem it, the land returns to him in the year of jubilee.

The houses of the Levites were surrounded by pasturelands for grazing sheep and making pens in them, for a distance of 500 meters on all sides, then the pasturelands were surrounded by fields belonging to them for a distance of a kilometer on all four sides. They cultivated these fields to eat from them and not to sell their crops, and it was not permitted to sell these pasturelands and fields, because they were their necessary sustenance and their portion from God.

Care for your heavenly house, that is, your place in eternity, and do not sell it because of any sin, for it is transient and ruins your life. And if you sold it by committing sin, hasten to repentance before the life symbolized by the year passes, so that you may always keep the goal of your life, which is your place in heaven.
Fallen in decay: He was unable to provide for his needs.
A stranger: A Jew of Gentile origin.
A sojourner: A Jew of Jewish origin.
That he may live with thee: He provides for his needs and lives as you live.

If one of the Jews became poor, then his fellow Jews ought to help him by lending him a sum of money or the foods he needs, without taking interest on these loans. God rebuked them for not carrying out this law, as in (Neh 5:2-12, Prov 28:8). Although this mercy was limited to a Jew toward a Jew, in the New Testament the heart of the Christian expands, so that he has mercy on everyone, because with spiritual maturity the Christian loves all people, since they are the image of God and His likeness (Jas 2:15-17).
The motive for not exploiting the poor when lending to him is the fear of God, who is the giver of gifts to all people, so that no one exploits another but has mercy on him and helps him.

God forbids interest on money such as gold and silver, and likewise interest on barter, which takes place by exchanging various foods and possessions, so that he takes no interest on them, which is called usury.

God reminds them that He is the Giver of the grace that was given to all His people, which is the possession of the land of Canaan with all its goods, so it is not right to exploit the poor, because all material things are from God.

Be compassionate toward the needy and do not take interest when you lend to them, and if you can, forgive what you lent them, or part of it, as long as the circumstances of the needy person do not allow him to repay the loan, knowing that God will bless you manifold for your mercy to him.

One of the Jews may suffer from poverty to the point that his family needs to sell him in order to pay what he owes of loans or so that his family may benefit from his price. The Law then requires the Jew who bought him to treat him gently as if he were a hired worker with him and not a slave.

He works in the house of the one who bought him as if he were a hired worker or a guest, and the one who bought him treats him well and gives him his food, the comfort of his body and his clothing. He remains thus in his service until six years are completed or the year of jubilee comes, whichever is nearer. This was covered in detail in (Ex 21:1-11) and was also confirmed in (Deut 15:
After the servant completes the years of service, he goes out, he and his sons, whom he fathered with the one who bought him, and returns free to his land.

God reminds them that they are all His servants, so it is not right that they be enslaved to anyone else. For He is the One who freed them from the bondage of Egypt and brought them out as His servants and free from the bondage of men, to live in the wilderness of Sinai and the Promised Land.
The deterrent against domineering over the servants and humiliating them is the fear of God, the owner of all His people, for wronging the children of God is wronging Him.

Be merciful to those who work for you, servants or subordinates, for they are all your brothers. Put yourself in their place so that you may feel for them and learn how to treat them, keeping before you God, who sees you at all times, for He is your Master who is able to take vengeance on you if you do not have mercy on the weak.
Bondmaids: Female slaves.

God permitted them to take servants from the nations around them, who would serve them all their lives and would not be released after a period as the Jews were. This was because the system of slavery was still prevalent in the world, and God wanted by it to teach them that whoever sells himself to sin and the worship of idols, like the Gentiles, is subject to material bondage, having accepted spiritual bondage, which is harder because it is bondage to sin. But they, the believers, enjoy the material freedom, which is a symbol of the spiritual freedom of the children of God, that is, their freedom from the bondage of sin.

In the New Testament the Church helped to address the problem of slavery by calling the masters to treat their servants gently, and she encouraged the rich to free their brothers who were slaves by paying the price of their freedom. She taught the slaves that they are free in God's sight as long as they keep away from sin, and that they are equal before God with the masters (Gal 3:28, Col 3:11). She even raised the slave to the highest ranks in the Church, which is the episcopate, like Onesimus, the slave of Philemon. She also called her servants to be slaves for the sake of Christ, to gather souls to Him and to serve all people (Titus 1:1, 2 Cor 4:5).
He permitted them to take servants from the foreign peoples who dwell around them and among them, and also from their own sons.

It is noted that God called them in the Law to be gentle with their servants and not to harm them lest they be punished (Ex 21:20), and God warned them against turning away from life with Him, lest He leave them to fall into slavery, as happened with Canaan, who saw the nakedness of Noah and so Noah cursed him and prophesied that he and his offspring would be servants (Gen 9:25, 26).

God gives them the right to bequeath their servants to their sons, so that just as the servants are their property, they are the property of their sons for all of life. All this concerns the servants from the nations, but the Jews work for a period until the sixth year or until the year of jubilee, as we mentioned, when they are set free.
Hand attains: He became rich.
Stranger or sojourner: One of the Gentiles, that is, non-Jews, who live among the Jews.
Thy brother that dwelleth by him be waxen poor: He became indebted to him.
The stock of the stranger's family: One of the relatives of this Gentile.

If a Jew became poor and borrowed from a rich non-Jewish person who lives among the Jews or near them, and so was compelled to sell himself to him, then one of the Jew's relatives should hasten to pay his price and free him, or, if this servant is able to gather money, he pays it and frees himself. The law ruled that if he is not freed, he is redeemed in the year of jubilee, but his relatives should not wait for the year of jubilee; rather, they should hasten to redeem him, because it is not right for a Jew to be a servant of men, since he is a servant of God.

When the Jew who was sold to the stranger is freed, the number of years remaining until the jubilee is counted, because the price of the sale increases if the jubilee is far off and decreases the nearer we come to it, as we mentioned before. So the difference in price between what he was bought for and what remains until the year of jubilee is paid to the buyer, that is, what remains of what he paid is paid to him after deducting the period that the Jew worked for him as a hired servant.

The stranger ought to treat the Jew who works for him as a hired servant and not domineer over him or humiliate him as a slave. These are the conditions for the work of the Jew with the non-Jew who bought him. And his brothers the Jews had to follow up the carrying out of this word until the money was available to them with which to free him completely.
The Law rules that if the Jew cannot redeem himself, or one of his relatives cannot redeem him, from the hand of the stranger, he receives his freedom in the year of jubilee.

God affirms that all His Jewish people are servants to Him because He freed them from the bondage of Egypt, so they are not to be enslaved to anyone. For He is the Lord their God who loves them and is jealous over them and does not want them to be humbled before any man. This is a symbol of a person's enslaving himself to sin, which is foreign to him, and he ought to hasten to repentance to God, that He may free him from it.

May you feel for your brothers who suffer pains and afflictions and try to help them and lighten their burdens, especially those fallen into various sins, so that you help them to know God and obtain their salvation in the Church. Blessing, discipline and mercy

In this chapter He summarizes the divine commands mentioned in the Book of Leviticus. In this verse He forbids them the worship of idols, among which they lived in Egypt and which would surround them in the land of Canaan, and He gives details of the idols or images, which are:
1- Making statues that they carve from any material in order to worship them.
2- Setting up pillars, which are walls or columns that remind them of the pagan gods so that they may worship them.
3- Stones carved in the form of the pagan gods.
What is meant is the prohibition of any form of idol worship, and rather the worship of the one God, the Creator of heaven and earth, as the second commandment stated (Ex 20:2, 3).
Here He calls them to two positive things in His worship, which are:

1- Setting apart the Sabbath day for the worship of God, as the fourth commandment stated (Ex 20:8-11). This also includes the sanctification of the seventh year and the year of jubilee (ch. 25:1-22). The sanctification of the Sabbath distinguishes them from the rest of the peoples and gives them God's blessing on the remaining days of the week.
2- Respect for the house of the Lord and offering sacrifices and prayers in it, because it is God's dwelling among them, so they enjoy His care and protection.

God sets a condition for receiving His blessings: not only knowing His commandments but applying them and acting by them. This shows God's concern for man's freedom and his obedience to His commandments, for they are the entrance to all the blessings, the most important of which He mentions in the following verses.

The first blessing is the coming down of rain from heaven at the times when the crops need it. This is essential in the cultivation of the land of Canaan, which depends on rain in addition to rivers. By this they obtain the produce of the field and the fruit of the trees, that is, they find their food. The rain is a symbol of the blessings of the Holy Spirit coming down to us from heaven, which we receive in the Church.

The second blessing is the abundance of the crops. Because of the abundance of the winter crops such as wheat and barley, the threshing of their grain, that is, separating the grain from the straw, continues from April to June, and so it joins with the time of the vintage, that is, the gathering of the fruits of the trees such as grapes and olives, which begins in June and continues until September, and this too joins with the time of winter sowing, which begins in the month of October. Thus the crops are abundant, so they are satisfied and thank God for His generosity.
He also promises them security as regards being satisfied with food and likewise protection from enemies, which He mentions in detail in the following verse.
The third blessing is peace and security, which is expressed by their sleeping a quiet sleep without any disturbance from two things, which are:
1- Enemies, in that He puts the awe of His people in their hearts, so they do not think of attacking them or seizing their crops and their spoils.
2- The wild beasts that were numerous in the land of Canaan, for He destroys them and drives them away from them.

If you obey God's commandments and are occupied with His love, trust that He supplies your needs and gives you the enjoyment of inner peace and gives you awe in the eyes of those around you, so that you remain in the enjoyment of fellowship with Him. So seek first the Kingdom of God and His righteousness, and know that the rest will be added to you.

The fourth blessing is strength and victory over enemies, if any of them dares and tries to attack them. They will conquer them, and they will flee before them, and they will drive them far from their land. There have been many examples of this, such as the victory of Moses over the Amalekites and of Joshua over the Canaanites.
Ten thousand: A myriad.

The power of God is manifested with His children, so that a small number of them can conquer a great number of enemies. He gives examples, namely the victory of five of the people of God over a hundred of the enemies and of a hundred of the people of God over ten thousand of the enemies. This happened often, such as the victory of three hundred men with Gideon over thousands of Midianites, the victory of Samson alone over great numbers of the Philistines, and the victory of Judas Maccabeus with a small number over the armies of the Greek empire.

The fifth blessing is the multiplication of offspring, which gives strength to the people of God. By this He fulfills His promise and His covenant with the fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and this means His care for them, which preserves them and multiplies them.
The old: The ancient.
The aged: The very ancient.

God blesses their harvests that they gather, so that they are very abundant, so much so that they eat from the crop of the past year until the crop of the new year comes, and much of the old crops may remain with them for several years, and when the new crops are gathered they are compelled to empty the storehouses of the old crops, as it says, "ye shall bring forth the old because of the new," in order to put in the new, that is, the goodness and the satisfaction are in great abundance.

The sixth blessing is God's good pleasure in them, as proved by His dwelling in their midst in the tabernacle of meeting or the temple of Solomon. When they disobeyed God, He refused to dwell in their midst, as happened at the end of the life of Eli the priest, when the Ark of the Covenant went to the Philistines, and as happened during the Babylonian captivity, when they destroyed the temple of God and Jerusalem.

Since God is pleased with them, He accompanies them in all their journeys and cares for them, and His name is called upon them, and they are a people special to Him and are distinguished by this from the rest of the peoples.

The bands of your yoke: The yoke is a crosswise piece of wood placed on the necks of two animals and tied to each neck by a rope called a band, and what is meant by breaking the bands of the yoke is freedom from slavery. And made you go upright: that is, erect, with the head held high in dignity, instead of the stooping of humiliation and bondage in Egypt, and what is meant is the dignity and exaltation that belong to the free.

God reminds them of His freeing them from the bondage of Egypt and their victory over it, and that therefore He is able to make them always victorious over their enemies in every place if they keep His commandments.
Break: You break the covenant and the compact.

On the other hand, God makes clear the punishments and curses that come upon His people if they refuse to keep His commandments and walk by them, and hate them, and break the covenant with Him of living as a people special to Him. He makes clear these disciplines in the following verses.

The first discipline is terror and disease. Instead of inner peace, fear fills their hearts, and diseases spread among them, such as tuberculosis and fevers of various kinds. These diseases affect the different members of the body, the most important of which are the eyes, which grow weak until a person loses his sight, and they also affect their souls and not only their bodies, so they suffer from many troubles and psychological disturbances. The second discipline is the plundering of their goods by the enemies. After they labor in sowing their crops, the enemies attack at the time of harvest or gathering and take their produce, so the people of God become poor and hungry.

The third discipline is defeat before the enemies. For if they disobey God and defy Him, God becomes an adversary to them, so they are defeated before their enemies however weak the latter are, and out of their fear they flee from the enemies even if the enemies do not pursue them, because terror fills their hearts, since God has forsaken them and has even become against them because of their sins, by which they rejected God.

Do not reject God and persist in sin and be careless about it, then afterward return to murmur because God has forsaken you. Know that the one who began the wrong is you and not God, so review yourself, and do not lose the most precious thing, which is the Kingdom, for the sake of trifling matters, which are the pleasures of this passing world and its evil desires.

If they accept the discipline and return to God in repentance, He forgives them, but if they persist in their sins, God increases the disciplines upon them sevenfold, that is, the fullness of discipline, until they repent and return.

The fourth discipline is humiliation. He removes from them their pride and dignity, which He gave them when He brought them out of the land of Egypt and by His care for them in the wilderness and when He gave them the land of Canaan to possess. So the enemies rise against them to occupy them and humble them.

The fifth discipline is the standing of nature against them, so that the heaven becomes like iron, that is, it gives them no rain, so cultivation fails and they suffer from hunger, and likewise the earth becomes like brass, that is, it loses its fertility and its ability to make the crops grow, so they are also exposed to hunger.

He explains and completes what He said in the previous verse concerning their loss of the produce of the land because of nature's defiance of them. However much they labor in cultivating the land, they reap nothing because of the land's defiance of them or because of pests, so they neither reap nor gather anything of the crops or the fruit of the trees, or they take very little, spoiled, which does not suffice them.
Here He repeats that if they do not submit to the divine discipline and repent of their sins, God will increase upon them the discipline and the blessings, perhaps they will take heed and repent.

The sixth discipline is the attack of wild beasts upon them, so that they devour their children and their cattle, and their number decreases and their strength weakens. This actually happened when the serpents bit the people in the days of Moses (Num 21:5, 6) and when two she bears devoured forty and two of the children who mocked Elisha (2 Kgs 2:23, 24).

Here He affirms to His people for a third time that if they persist in their sins, He will continue to discipline them and even multiply it sevenfold, that is, the fullness of discipline, so that they may submit and return from their sins.

Here He affirms their defeat before the enemies, who strike them with the sword and kill them, in addition to the spread of plagues with various diseases that finish them. By this God breaks His covenant with them of blessing and protection, because they transgressed His commandments, so He forsook them and the enemies and the plagues attacked them.
The seventh discipline is the famine, which has been referred to and which resulted from the previous disciplines.

Because bread is the basis of food, He calls it the staff of bread, since a person leans and relies on a staff, so God breaks the staff of bread, that is, a famine occurs. He expresses the details of this famine by saying that the oven, that is, the furnace that would suffice for the baking of one woman or one house, will, because of the scarcity of the crops and the lack of flour except a little in every house, suffice for the baking of ten houses or ten women. He affirms the famine by saying that the bread will be given to people by weight because of its scarcity, so they return it, that is, they turn it over in their hands with care, and weigh a small amount for each person, so that he does not eat more than it because of hunger.

Here God repeats to His people that if they disobey Him and transgress His commandments, He will forsake them and will also walk with them in fierce wrath, so He permits disciplines sevenfold upon them because of their defiance and rebellion, perhaps they will repent.

From the severity of the hunger that God permits, a person loses his natural feelings and becomes like a ravening beast, so he slaughters his sons and eats them in order to live. This actually happened in the siege of Jerusalem by Babylon (Lam 4:9, 10) and in the siege of Jerusalem by the Romans in AD 70.

The eighth discipline is the destruction of the altars of the idols that were set up on the hills and the images of the sun that they hung on wooden columns, which are the posts, or placed in houses for the worship of the sun. God also permits them to be killed by the sword and their corpses to be cast upon the carcasses of the animals that they offered on the altars of the idols, that is, they die in their evil by forsaking God and worshiping foreign gods.

God continues His discipline by destroying the cities and likewise the holy places, which are His temple in Jerusalem, as happened during the attack of Babylon and its destruction of the temple and Jerusalem, and as also happened when the Romans destroyed the temple. God adds that He will not accept their sacrifices that they offer to Him, that is, He rejects their worship because of their persistence in evil.

As a continuation of the blow of destruction, the land becomes desolate, that is, ruined, and wild beasts dwell in it, so that their enemies who occupy them cannot bear to live in their desolate lands and are amazed at this ruin to which the cities of the people of God have come.
I will draw out a sword: I will take it out of its sheath to kill many with it, and what is meant is that He permits the enemies, whom God regards as His sword, to kill them.

As an extension of the ruin of their cities, they are scattered in the countries of the world, where the enemies carry them off after killing many of them, and so their lands and their cities remain ruined.
Her sabbaths: What is meant by the sabbath is the seventh year, in which the commandment ordered that the land not be cultivated.

The people of God neglected for a long time to carry out His commandments by not cultivating the land in the seventh year and in the year of jubilee, that is, the fiftieth year. So God permitted the land to be ruined and not cultivated, in place of the seventh year in which they ought not to have sown, and the captivity lasts long enough, and the land lies ruined without cultivation, until the years in which they ought not to have cultivated it are fulfilled, but they transgressed God's commandments and cultivated it.

By this they lost the blessing of God that He used to give them in the sixth year, then their lands were ruined for many years and their cities too were destroyed, and they came under the divine wrath.
Faintness: Cowardice and fear.

Here He affirms the first discipline, which is the casting of fear into the hearts of the people of God while they are captives. They fear though no one frightens them, so that even the movement of a leaf of a tree in the wind disturbs their hearts and they flee though their enemies do not pursue them, because fear has filled their hearts.

He continues the discipline of fear that comes upon them. They flee though no one chases them, because of the intensity of their anxiety, and as they flee one stumbles upon another and they fall to the ground as they run. Thus they continue in their defeat before the enemies though the enemies have left them, but fear continues to disturb them and drives them.
Thus the people of God grow weak and many of them perish in the land of the enemies, and they lose their lineages, their nationality and their worship, and so become worthless.

The remaining captives of the people of God perish in the lands of the enemies because of their sins and the sins of their fathers in which they continued, whether by the worship of idols or by the many unclean lusts.
Their uncircumcised hearts: that is, those not circumcised, and what is meant is not believing and renewed by faith to live in purity with God.

After showing His blessings for those who obey His commandments and His disciplines for those who transgress them, He gives hope to those who transgressed against Him and understood and accepted His disciplines, so they repented and returned to Him, and He embraces them with His mercies. This repentance means confessing their sins and the sins of their fathers in which they continued. By this they transgressed against God, so God walked contrary to them, that is, He forsook them and permitted their discipline and their scattering in the countries of their enemies, who carried them away from their land. By this confession they declare the return of their hearts to faith and their acceptance of the discipline they deserve because of their disobedience.
I will remember My covenant: This does not mean that God had forgotten, but a divine declaration that He will fulfill His covenant and His promise.

The mercies of God to His repentant children appear in that He fulfills to them His promises of caring for them and protecting them, as He promised their father Jacob, the father of the tribes, and their forefathers Isaac and Abraham (Gen 22:16-18), (Gen 26:1-6), (Gen 35:9-15). And He brings them back to the Promised Land after their captivity.
Enjoy her sabbaths: Explained before in (v. 35), that is, it is not cultivated, in place of the seventh year in which they did not sanctify the land to God by not cultivating it.
Desolate: The land remains desolate, that is, uncultivated.
They despised My judgments: They disobeyed and refused to obey My judgments.

God has mercy on His repentant children after He disciplined them by moving them from their lands at the hands of the enemies. They left the land uncultivated as a result of their transgression in former times and their disobedience to the commandment of the seventh year, in which He commanded them not to cultivate the land. So as a punishment they leave their land against their will, uncultivated and desolate for long years.
I have not abhorred them: I have not forsaken them and withheld My fatherhood from them.
To break My covenant: To violate My covenant.

The mercies of God also appear in His not hating His people when they disobeyed Him. He scattered them in the countries of the enemies but did not destroy them, and He kept waiting until they repented, so that He would fulfill His covenant and His fatherhood and care for them and bring them back to their land in glory and honor.

God's tenderness toward you continues even while you are in sin, and He awaits your return to embrace you with His mercies. You will not find tenderness like His in the world, so do not delay repentance and returning to Him.

God affirms that He will fulfill His promises to the first fathers, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and so He will have mercy on His repentant people whom He brought out of the land of Egypt and will restore His care and protection to them.
Here God concludes His speech, saying that what has gone before are God's laws for His children, that they may live by them.
Vows, firstborn, devoted things and tithes (1) Vows:

A – Of persons (vv. 1-8) 1 And the LORD spake unto Moses, saying, 2 "Speak unto the children of Israel, and say unto them, When a man shall make a singular vow, the persons shall be for the LORD by thy estimation. 3 And thy estimation shall be of the male from twenty years old even unto sixty years old, even thy estimation shall be fifty shekels of silver, after the shekel of the sanctuary. 4 And if it be a female, then thy estimation shall be thirty shekels. 5 And if it be from five years old even unto twenty years old, then thy estimation shall be of the male twenty shekels, and for the female ten shekels. 6 And if it be from a month old even unto five years old, then thy estimation shall be of the male five shekels of silver, and for the female thy estimation shall be three shekels of silver. 7 And if it be from sixty years old and above; if it be a male, then thy estimation shall be fifteen shekels, and for the female ten shekels. 8 But if he be poorer than thy estimation, then he shall present himself before the priest, and the priest shall value him; according to his ability that vowed shall the priest value him."

According to your estimation: that is, your assessment and approval of the vow so that it accords with the conditions of the Law (vv. 3-8). After Moses, it was the priest who assessed and approved the vow.

A vow is a promise to offer a gift to God if He grants a person his request, or it is an offering of love given in thanksgiving to God for His kindnesses and in striving to cling to God. The promise is either to do something positive or to abstain from something. Vows were made of persons, animals, birds or fields, and in this part he speaks about vows of persons.

The one who declared the vow was the person himself or those responsible for him, such as his parents. It was required that he be free and not a slave, so that he would have the ability to carry out his vow. If a woman made a vow while in her father's house, her father's consent was required, and likewise in her husband's house her husband's consent was necessary. But if she was a widow or divorced and lived alone or with her children, she could declare a vow.

It was also necessary that the vow be declared aloud, so that a person would not doubt the thoughts that had come to him, and that it be made from wealth of honorable source. A vow is voluntary, but if a person makes a vow he must fulfill it (Deut 23:21-23; Eccl 5:4, 5). Vows have been known from ancient times: Jacob vowed to God (Gen 28:20-22); they are also found among the other pagan peoples, as the sailors who were with Jonah vowed (Jon 1:16); and they continue in Christianity, as Paul vowed (Acts 18:18).
A shekel of silver: about 15 grams.
The shekel of the sanctuary: the exact shekel, a sample of which was kept in the house of the Lord, in order to regulate the scales so that they would not be false.

The first kind of vow of persons is the vow of a man aged from twenty to sixty years, which is the period of bodily strength, in which he is enlisted for war. For him fifty shekels of silver are offered, and if he is unable to fulfill his vow, he is consecrated to the service of God.

The offering of silver instead of the person consecrating himself is a symbol of Christ's redemption, because silver is a symbol of the Word of God, that is, Christ, for it is He who redeems the lives of His children.
In Christianity, after the mystery of redemption has been made clear, a person's vowing himself means consecrating his life to God, such as the vow of virginity or the vow of monasticism.

In the case of a female vowed at the same age, that is, from twenty to sixty years, the silver offered for her is only thirty shekels, because her bodily strength, and therefore her ability to serve and work, is less than that of a man, in addition to the woman's responsibilities in caring for her house and her children.
If the person vowed is between five and twenty years of age, his ability to work is less, so for a male twenty shekels are offered and for a female ten shekels.

If the one vowed is a child between one month and five years of age, his service is either nonexistent or very slight, so five shekels are offered for him if he is male, or three if she is female. There are examples of a vow at this age, such as Samuel (1 Sam 1:22-24), Samson (Judg 13:5) and John the Baptist (Lk 1:15).

If the person vowed is more than sixty years old, his effort is less, so for a male fifteen shekels are offered and for a female ten shekels. It is noticeable that the amount of silver for the female has increased here and become two thirds of the man's, because a woman's ability to work in old age is often greater than in the days of childhood.

If the one who vowed is poor and cannot offer the silver in the amounts mentioned above, he stands before the priest, who examines his financial means and determines for him the amount of money that he is able to offer to God. Note the mercy of God, who has compassion on His poor children and rejoices in their gifts even if they are very small.

If you have not vowed your life to God, do not forget that you are wholly His possession, for it is He who redeemed you. So consecrate your heart to love Him, strive to be with Him, and drive out every evil desire that defiles your heart.

B- Of animals (vv. 9-13) 9"And if it be a beast, whereof men bring an offering unto the LORD, all that any man giveth of such unto the LORD shall be holy. 10 He shall not alter it, nor change it, a good for a bad, or a bad for a good: and if he shall at all change beast for beast, then it and the exchange thereof shall be holy. 11 And if it be any unclean beast, of which they do not offer a sacrifice unto the LORD, then he shall present the beast before the priest: 12 And the priest shall value it, whether it be good or bad: as thou valuest it, who art the priest, so shall it be. 13 But if he will at all redeem it, then he shall add a fifth part thereof unto thy estimation.
Whereof men bring an offering unto the LORD: that is, of the clean animals that are permitted to be offered as sacrifices to God, namely cattle, sheep and goats.
Holy: set apart for God.

If a person vows to offer one of the animals to God if God grants him his request, he must offer exactly what he vowed and may not substitute anything for it, and it is required that it be one of the animals permitted to be offered to God, that is, clean animals.

Here he stresses the necessity of fulfilling the vow just as its maker pronounced it, and not substituting another animal for it. If he does this, that is, offers another animal, he is obliged to offer the vow also as he pronounced it, that is, to offer two animals: the one he offered first and the one he vowed. The priests could sell these vowed animals to the people who wished to offer sacrifices to God, and the price was placed in the house of the Lord. Offering the very vow that its maker pronounced is a symbol that God knows us by our names and accepts no substitute for our souls, for we have a place in His heart that no one else can fill; His fatherhood loves us and seeks each one of us specifically.

If a person vows one of the unclean animals, such as the donkey, or an animal with a defect, the animal is made to stand before the priest to value it, and the one who vowed pays the price the priest has set into the house of the Lord. This is a symbol that God does not accept an unclean gift from our hands, that is, one that we have obtained from an unlawful source.

If the maker of the vow desires to keep the animal he vowed, this is considered a fault and an excessive desire, so God accepts his vow by the payment of the animal's price, but he adds to it a fifth, because he desired it after he had vowed it to God.

If Christ did not withhold His life from you but gave it for you on the Cross, then do not withhold your life or anything you own, but be ready to offer everything to God as an expression of your love.

C- Of houses (vv. 14, 15) 14"And when a man shall sanctify his house to be holy unto the LORD, then the priest shall estimate it, whether it be good or bad: as the priest shall estimate it, so shall it stand. 15 And if he that sanctified it will redeem his house, then he shall add the fifth part of the money of thy estimation unto it, and it shall be his.
If a person vows his house to God, the priest values its price, the priest sells it, and he offers its price to the house of God.
If the one who vowed his house to God desires to keep his house, this is considered an excessive desire, and therefore he pays the price of the house and also a fifth in addition.

If the priest was the voice of God in the Old Testament, to guide the people and assess their life, how much more in the New Testament, through the sacrament of confession, in which God declares His voice to you through the tongue of your father of confession. So present your life before him in repentance, and pray to God, and He will guide you through the tongue of the priest, and you will rejoice in God's leading of your life.

D- Of fields (vv. 16-25) 16"And if a man shall sanctify unto the LORD some part of a field of his possession, then thy estimation shall be according to the seed thereof: an homer of barley seed shall be valued at fifty shekels of silver. 17 If he sanctify his field from the year of jubile, according to thy estimation it shall stand. 18 But if he sanctify his field after the jubile, then the priest shall reckon unto him the money according to the years that remain, even unto the year of the jubile, and it shall be abated from thy estimation. 19 And if he that sanctified the field will in any wise redeem it, then he shall add the fifth part of the money of thy estimation unto it, and it shall be assured to him. 20 And if he will not redeem the field, or if he have sold the field to another man, it shall not be redeemed any more. 21 But the field, when it goeth out in the jubile, shall be holy unto the LORD, as a field devoted; the possession thereof shall be the priest's. 22 And if a man sanctify unto the LORD a field which he hath bought, which is not of the fields of his possession; 23 Then the priest shall reckon unto him the worth of thy estimation, even unto the year of the jubile: and he shall give thine estimation in that day, as a holy thing unto the LORD.

24 "In the year of the jubile the field shall return unto him of whom it was bought, even to him to whom the possession of the land did belong. 25 And all thy estimations shall be according to the shekel of the sanctuary: twenty gerahs shall be the shekel."
Homer: equal to ten ephahs, and the ephah equals 22.9 liters.
If a person vows a part of his field that he inherited from his fathers, the priest values it so that it may be sold to any person who wishes to buy it, and the price is offered to the Temple.

The price is determined according to the amount of seed sufficient for sowing it. An homer of barley seed was valued at fifty shekels of silver, so one calculates how much the land needs, that is, how many homers of seed.
If a person vows a part of his field in the year of jubile, the priest values the price of the field, it is sold to whoever wishes to buy it, and the price is paid to the house of God.

The preceding case in (v. 17) is a vow in the year of jubile. But if a field is vowed after the year of jubile, the priest values its price, and it is less, since years have passed from which the buyer did not benefit, and fewer than 49 years remain until the year of jubile, in which the field will return to God and the priest will receive it (v. 20). The buyer pays the price to the priest; this is the value of the vow, and he works the land and takes its produce until the year of jubile.

If the one who vowed desires the field that he vowed to God and wishes to redeem it for himself, he pays a price greater than its sale price that the priest set, by an amount of a fifth, as happened in the case of the beast and the house (vv. 13, 15).

If the owner of the field does not redeem his field for himself by paying its price with the addition of a fifth, and the priest sold it to any person, then in the year of jubile the field returns to God and the priest receives it to oversee its cultivation and harvest, and it does not return to its owner but becomes holy, that is, set apart for God.

This means that in this case the Law encourages the owner of the field, who was in some difficulty and made a vow to God that He might resolve it for him, that after he has pronounced the vow and before the priest sells the field to any person, he or one of his relatives should hasten to redeem the field and return it to its owner, so that he may hold fast to the inheritance of the fathers, which is a symbol of the eternal inheritance.

Hold fast to the teachings of the Church, the commandments of your parents, and every good thing you have learned, for it is the true inheritance from the fathers that guarantees you the way of life with God.

If a person buys a field from another, and he will of course return it to its owner in the year of jubile, and then vows it to God during the period of his ownership of this field and his enjoyment of its produce, he gives the price of the produce until the year of jubile to the house of the Lord; this is the fulfillment of the vow. The valuation of the field's price until the year of jubile is according to the valuation of the priest, who is the voice of God and just in his judgments. In the year of jubile the field returns to its original owner, from whom the maker of the vow bought it, so that every person may keep the inheritance of his fathers and the portion of every tribe may remain fixed.
Gerah: equal to the weight of a carob seed, or 0.75 of a gram.

God admonishes Moses and all the priests after him that the unit of valuation is to be the shekel of the sanctuary, which equals twenty gerahs, that is, about 15 grams. The meaning is that the unit of valuation should be exact, to ensure a just and precise valuation.

Here he affirms the law of offering the firstborn of animals to God, that is, the first offspring of an animal. It is not right to vow this to Him, because it already belongs to God and must be offered to the Temple. All this concerns clean animals such as the ox and the sheep.

Be careful to offer to God the firstfruits of your day, beginning with prayer before any other work. Would that you join prayer with reading the Holy Bible, choosing a verse to memorize and repeat throughout the day and try to apply in your life. And know that a spiritual beginning with God will give you peace throughout the day and keep you from the snares of the devil.
The firstborn of all animals must be offered to God, but unclean animals such as the donkey may not be offered to the Temple, so in this case one of these things is done:
1- The animal is sold and the price is given to the Temple.
2- If the owner of the animal loves to keep it, this means that he has a desire to possess, so he pays its price, a fifth is added to it, and it is offered to the priests.
3- The animal is redeemed with a lamb, as the Book of Exodus mentions (Ex 13:13).

God used to command the devoting to destruction of some wicked and dangerous peoples because of the multitude of their evils. These had to be put to death and could not be redeemed, as He commanded the devoting of the Canaanite peoples when Joshua entered to possess the land, and he fought them and killed them (Deut 7:1-4; Josh 9, 10, 11). God also commanded the devoting of some persons, even if they were kings, such as Agag king of Amalek, whom the prophet Samuel killed (1 Sam 15:32, 33). As for animals and possessions such as silver and gold, devoting them means offering them to the Lord, and they cannot be sold or redeemed. Whoever transgresses this law brings God's great anger upon himself, as happened with Achan the son of Carmi, who took possessions from Jericho that had to be devoted to God, and God commanded that he be put to death (Josh 7:25). That is, the devoting comes by the command of God or by the judgment of the judges according to the Law.

Obey the guidance of your father of confession by cutting off everything that leads to sin, however precious and dear it is in your eyes or however much your soul desires it, for your salvation is more important than anything in life.

God commanded the offering of tithes from all the produce of the land and of the animals. Here he speaks of the tithes of the produce of the field, which are the grains and all the products of the planted crops, in addition to the tithes of the fruit of the trees, and these are offered to God every year. The produce of the field was offered after threshing, that is, it was offered as grain, and the fruit was either offered fresh, or the grapes could be offered as juice and the olives as oil, which is easy to store without spoiling. The produce of the field was offered in the Temple of God (Deut 12:11), and if it was far from them in the land of Canaan, it could be sold and its price offered in Jerusalem (Deut 14:24-27). Of these tithes the priests, the Levites, the poor and the needy would eat, because the priests and the Levites had no portion in the land like the other tribes.

The tithes of the third year were offered by each person in his own city to the poor and the Levites (Deut 14:28, 29). The seventh year had no tithes because the land is not sown in it, and likewise the year of jubile, that is, the fiftieth year.

Tithes were known among men before their appearance in the Law of Moses, for Abraham offered tithes of the spoils he had taken in his war with the kings to Melchizedek (Gen 14:20). And Jacob vowed to offer tithes to God when He appeared to him on the ladder (Gen 28:22).
If a person desires to keep the tenth of his produce, which he ought to have offered to God, he must pay its price to the Temple and add a fifth to the price, because of his love for material things.

As for the tithes of animals, each year they would gather the young born among them and pass them one by one through a narrow gate, while the shepherd counted with his rod, and when he reached the tenth he took it and offered it to God.

The tenth of the animals is offered without examination, and if its owner finds it good and fat, it is not right for him to exchange it for a weak one, for this is a kind of theft directed against God. If he exchanges it, he is obliged to offer the good animal and also the weak animal that he put in its place, that is, to offer two animals, that is, the fifth, because of the sin of the love of money and the sin of theft. And even if he exchanged the weak tenth animal for a good animal, he offers both as well, so that the Law would not give anyone an opportunity to deceive and exchange the animal for any personal purpose.
He concludes this chapter, and indeed the whole Book of Leviticus, affirming that what precedes is the Law that God gave to Moses at Mount Sinai in the tabernacle of meeting (ch. 1:1).

The blessing of offering tithes is very great, for it is an expression of your love for God. He has no need of material things, but He rejoices in your love for Him and your care for the needs of the Church and of all the needy. God is not indebted to anyone, and He will bless you, as He promised, with heavenly blessings beyond what you imagine.
